comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to retain the existing grace period of up to 60 days for H-1B workers who unexpectedly lose their employment.

The 60-day grace period serves an important and practical purpose. It provides a reasonable amount of time for individuals and their families to responsibly conclude their affairs in the United States following an unexpected loss of employment. Rather, it provides a limited transition period to make necessary arrangements and depart the country in an orderly and lawful manner.

Losing a job unexpectedly is already a significant personal and financial hardship. However, leaving the United States is not something that can realistically be accomplished overnight. Individuals and families need time to vacate apartments or terminate leases, arrange the sale or shipment of personal belongings, close utility accounts, settle financial obligations, coordinate school transitions for children, and make international travel arrangements. These responsibilities require time, planning, and coordination, particularly for families with children.

International travel arrangements can also be complicated and expensive, especially when an entire family must relocate on short notice. Securing affordable flights, coordinating travel schedules, arranging transportation of belongings, and addressing outstanding contractual and financial commitments cannot always be completed within a few days.

The existing grace period also serves an important purpose in helping individuals avoid unintentionally accumulating unlawful presence or falling into an immigration compliance issue simply because they were unable to arrange their departure immediately after losing employment. Providing a clearly defined and limited transition period encourages individuals to remain compliant with U.S. immigration laws and make an orderly departure rather than face circumstances that could lead to unintended immigration violations.

Furthermore, the impact of an unexpected job loss extends beyond the individual H-1B worker. Families may have children enrolled in local schools, ongoing rental or mortgage obligations, vehicles, household possessions, health insurance arrangements, and other commitments established over several years of living and working in the United States. These families deserve a reasonable opportunity to responsibly close these obligations and transition to life outside the country.

The current up-to-60-day grace period is a modest and reasonable safeguard. It does not provide an indefinite extension of stay or permit unauthorized employment. It simply recognizes the practical realities of relocating an individual or an entire family internationally and provides sufficient time to comply with immigration requirements.

I respectfully request that DHS and USCIS retain the existing up-to-60-day grace period for H-1B workers following involuntary job loss. Eliminating or substantially reducing this period would create unnecessary hardship and could make it more difficult for otherwise law-abiding individuals and families to depart the United States in an orderly and compliant manner.

Thank you for considering this comment and recognizing the importance of providing H-1B workers and their families with a reasonable period to conclude their affairs and depart the United States responsibly.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly urges DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sam King
comments.commentText: Don't get rid of the grace period.  I know and have worked with H1B visa holders.  Disrupting their lives and adding more uncertainty is cruel.  It isn't reflective of who we should be as a country.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sudip Paul
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period"

I oppose this rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I have lived in the United States for 16 years, in H-1B status since 2015, and have changed employers four times under H-1B portability. I own my home in San Jose, California, and my wife and I are raising our daughter, a U.S. citizen, here. For most of those years, a layoff under this rule would have ended my status and my wife's the following day. We could not have sold a house or withdrawn a child from school in a day, and our daughter would have left the only country she is a citizen of. Few employers will hire into a role that requires a consular petition, weeks abroad and a six-figure fee if the $100,000 payment returns. Today I have a pending adjustment of status application that is likely to remain pending for years. The rule still reaches me: my H-1B status is the only fallback if that application is denied, and a layoff would strip it the same day. Sixteen years of work and community would turn on the timing of a layoff notice, not on any decision of mine.

My objections, each tied to a section of the NPRM:

1. Statute (Sections IV.A-B). INA 214(n) lets an H-1B worker start new employment once a nonfrivolous petition is filed "before the date of expiration of the period of stay authorized," the I-94 date. Congress did not require the worker to be employed on the day of filing. The grace period is what makes that provision usable after a layoff: a Labor Condition Application alone takes about seven working days (20 CFR 655.730(b)) and a filed petition takes weeks, so a zero-day window makes every involuntary termination a mandatory departure. That is not alignment; it is a condition the statute does not contain.

2. The regulatory impact analysis (RIA) (Section V.A) cannot support the "not economically significant" finding. DHS monetizes one cost, $204-$301 per court visit; everything else is "Not Estimated."
(a) Population. DHS proxies job loss with revoked I-129s (65,752 per year), admits it cannot separate voluntary moves from layoffs, and counts only petitions filed within 60 days after the old employer's withdrawal rather than after termination, excluding those who ported fastest. The resulting 3,795 is called an "upper bound"; it is a lower bound, omitting I-539 filers (2,733 in FY2025) and working H-4, L-2 and E spouses.
(b) Wages. DHS found a $131,000 median wage for grace-period porters and never multiplied. 3,795 x $131,000 = $497 million in annual wages at stake; departure and consular re-entry plausibly adds 8-16 weeks of absence, or $76-$153 million per year from this undercounted group alone, before dependents, employers or removal proceedings. That crosses the $100 million threshold of E.O. 12866 section 3(f)(1).
(c) NTAs. DHS expects NTAs to rise only marginally from 37 in FY2025. But under the rule every post-termination filer is out of status, and under USCIS's February 2025 NTA policy a denied I-539 (2,733 workers in FY2025, plus every dependent) produces an NTA; I-129 beneficiaries are spared only by a revocable policy exception. The $204-$301 per hearing also omits counsel, repeat hearings and the 3/10-year bars.

3. Burden (Section IV.C). The "over 1.9 million" filings since FY2018 is the whole caseload; Table 3 shows about 5,300 post-termination filings per year, roughly 45,000 over the same period, under 3 percent of that. Burden likely rises: the filings do not disappear; each becomes a request to excuse a status violation under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4), the same kind of individualized discretionary review DHS calls burdensome, now in every case, plus the NTAs and EOIR referrals DHS admits.

4. Reliance (Section IV.D). DHS calls reliance "misplaced" because the period is discretionary. DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), rejected that reasoning for DACA. USCIS's own December 2022 guidance told workers they could remain for up to 60 days. Workers maintaining H-1B status as the fallback for a pending adjustment of status application relied on it most.

5. Footnote 19 strikes the grace-period reference from 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i), so compelling-circumstances EAD eligibility ends the day a job does, for a benefit designed for job loss. It receives no analysis. Withdraw it, or add an express 60-day filing window.

6. Alternatives (Section IV.E). It rejects every alternative for the same reason: it would still let a worker remain after employment ends. That is the proposal restated as its own justification. DHS should analyze a fixed, non-discretionary 60-day period from an employer-documented last day of employment, retaining the period for involuntary terminations, or at a minimum treating I-129, I-539 and I-765 filings within 60 days of cessation as timely.

Request: withdraw the rule; failing that, adopt a fixed non-discretionary period and publish a revised RIA with monetized ranges for re-comment.

Sudip Paul, San Jose, California
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the rule, stating it would harm families and workers during unexpected layoffs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lakshmi Kanth Mohan
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strongest opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant visa holders like myself.

I have lived, worked, and paid taxes in the United States legally on an H-1B visa for 10 years. During this past decade, my family and I have rooted our entire lives here. I bought a home, invested deeply in our local community, and have been patiently waiting in the employment-based Green Card backlogs for over 9 years to complete our lawful path to permanent residency.

My two children were raised here—America is the only home they know, love, and understand. They go to school here, have their friends here, and dream their dreams in English. The 60-day grace period is not a loophole or an unnecessary administrative buffer; it is our family’s single lifeline. In the volatile world of employment, sudden layoffs can happen through no fault of the worker. A 60-day grace period provides just enough time to secure new employment, transfer a visa, and avoid uprooting American-raised children overnight from their schools, homes, and community.

Eliminating this safety net forces families who have contributed a decade of their lives to the U.S. economy into immediate panic and potential departure upon a single career disruption. It effectively tells law-abiding, highly skilled immigrants who have built real lives, bought homes, and raised kids here that their decade of loyalty and legal compliance can end in a single day.

Please do not destroy the American Dream for families like mine who have done everything right by the book. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to preserve the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders and their dependents.
comments.reason: The commenter argues strongly against eliminating the grace period, stating it serves as a vital lifeline for families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Angelina Jolie
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose removing the 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), and I ask DHS to keep it in place. In Section IV.D, DHS invites comments on reliance interests. This comment explains how H-1B, L-1, and other workers and their families depend on this period.

When a worker is laid off or a project ends, it is usually sudden and not the worker’s fault. These workers have lived here lawfully for years. They have built lives in the United States: their children attend local schools, and they have signed loans and leases in good faith. If status ends the day after employment ends, they have no time to wind down those obligations responsibly. The 60-day period gives them time to plan the next step, whether that means finding a new employer, changing status, or leaving the country in an orderly way.

1. Financial obligations such as car loans and lease agreements.
Many visa holders have a car loan with monthly payments and a residential lease. Selling a car or paying off a loan takes time. If a worker has to leave immediately, they may be forced to sell at a loss or leave the loan unpaid. Breaking a lease early usually means an early-termination penalty, often about two months’ rent. With 60 days, a worker can sell the car, close the loan, give proper notice to the landlord, and settle utilities and bank accounts. Without that time, the people hurt include American lenders, landlords, and businesses, not just the worker.

2. Children’s education and family stability.
Many affected workers have children enrolled in U.S. schools. Taking a child out of school with no notice disrupts their education and their mental well-being. Sixty days lets the family get school records and transfer certificates, finish a grading period where possible, arrange admission in another school or country, and help the children prepare emotionally for the move. Families need this time to understand what is happening and adjust to it.

3. An orderly departure instead of default.
The grace period protects people who have followed the rules. It lets them meet every obligation and leave or change status lawfully, rather than becoming defaulters on loans and leases or being pushed into an unplanned status violation. That serves the program-integrity goals DHS cites, because it encourages careful compliance. Without the period, people who did nothing wrong could be left with debts, damaged credit, and possible immigration consequences. DHS’s own analysis acknowledges lost income and possible Notices to Appear for affected beneficiaries.

Requested action: Keep 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and the up-to-60-day grace period as it is. The period was adopted in the 2016 AC21 rule, and workers and families have relied on it for nearly a decade. It costs little, it already gives USCIS discretion to shorten or eliminate it in individual cases, and it gives lawful workers the time they need to plan responsibly and leave in an orderly way. For a visa holder, this time is essential.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes removing the grace period and argues it harms workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period. This provision serves an important purpose by allowing reasonable flexibility and consideration of individual circumstances. Unexpected situations, financial difficulties, administrative delays, and circumstances beyond someone's control should not automatically result in penalties. Removing this option would create unnecessary hardship and take away an important opportunity for individuals. I urge decision-makers to retain the 60-day grace period and preserve the flexibility to make fair, reasonable, and balanced decisions.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to eliminating the grace period and urges decision-makers to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it and keep 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) in place.

1. Workers usually don't choose when their job ends. Most loss of status under this rule would come from layoffs, restructurings, or employer closures, not from anything the worker did. The grace period gives a skilled worker who followed every rule a short window to find a new sponsor, change status, or leave in an orderly way. If it is removed, a worker laid off on a Friday would be out of status by Monday through no fault of their own.

2. Immediate departure is not realistic, and the harm reaches whole families. These workers and their dependents have leases, mortgages, children enrolled in school, vehicles, and household goods. They cannot wind up a life in the U.S. in a day. Dependents, including H-4 spouses, many of whom work for U.S. employers, would lose status at the same moment. These are exactly the kind of reliance interests that settled law requires an agency to weigh seriously before reversing a policy (see FCC v. Fox Television Stations; DHS v. Regents of the University of California). The NPRM does not show that DHS weighed them adequately against its stated goals.

3. It undercuts portability that Congress created. Congress gave H-1B workers portability so they could move between employers. A new employer needs time to prepare a petition. Without any grace period, a gap of just a few days between jobs could end a worker's ability to stay. That frustrates the purpose of portability.

4. DHS's own analysis contradicts its claim that this reduces burden. The NPRM justifies the rule by citing reduced complexity. But DHS itself expects that USCIS would devote resources to issuing Notices to Appear and starting removal proceedings, and that employers of workers who depart would lose productivity for a time. Moving cases from a short, discretionary determination into the already backlogged immigration courts increases burden on the government as a whole. It does not reduce it.

5. Program-integrity concerns have narrower fixes. The grace period is already discretionary, so USCIS can deny it where there is fraud or misconduct. If adjudication is burdensome, DHS could set standardized evidence for showing when employment ended, or provide clearer guidance. Removing protection for everyone is out of proportion to the problem.

6. It hurts U.S. competitiveness. Employers compete globally for scarce talent. A system where a single layoff forces a family to leave immediately makes the U.S. less attractive to the engineers, researchers, physicians, and executives these programs exist to attract. It also raises recruitment and replacement costs for U.S. employers.

Requested action: Withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds anyway, it should keep the grace period for workers whose employment ended involuntarily and for their dependents, and it should address reliance interests and alternatives in the final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and asks DHS to keep the current grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a lawful permanent resident who has worked in the United States for the past 17 years. I oppose the proposed removal of the discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to retain this protection because eliminating it could increase employers’ ability to pressure foreign workers, discourage reporting of workplace misconduct, and undermine fair working conditions for U.S. workers.

Eliminating the grace period could give employers excessive power over workers.

When a worker’s immigration status depends on employment, the threat of termination already carries consequences beyond the loss of a paycheck. Removing the grace period would intensify those consequences by creating the prospect of immediate departure unless the worker has another lawful basis to remain.

An abusive manager could use that fear to discourage employees from questioning unreasonable demands or reporting mistreatment. Workers may hesitate to raise concerns even through internal human resources channels if they believe retaliation could abruptly disrupt their ability—and their family’s ability—to remain in the country. My concern is that this proposal could create conditions of coercive dependence on an employer.

These pressures could also harm U.S. workers and responsible employers.

If foreign workers feel compelled to tolerate abusive conditions, excessive demands, or retaliation, the consequences can extend to their coworkers. U.S. citizens and permanent residents who are more able to raise concerns could face pressure to accept the same conditions or risk being viewed as less cooperative.

Employers willing to exploit immigration-related vulnerability could also gain an unfair advantage over employers that maintain fair workplace standards. DHS should evaluate whether eliminating the grace period would encourage competition based on workers’ fear of losing status and weaken workplace accountability.

A limited transition period supports responsible planning and orderly departure.

Although H-1B classification is temporary, it permits dual intent: eligible workers may maintain H-1B status while pursuing lawful permanent residence. Families make housing, schooling, and financial decisions around their authorized stay and the immigration processes available to them.

A sudden layoff can disrupt those arrangements without warning. The existing discretionary period of up to 60 days, limited by the remaining authorized validity period, provides time to address practical responsibilities. These may include ending a lease, arranging travel, handling financial obligations, and coordinating a family’s departure. For workers eligible to pursue another lawful immigration option, it also provides a limited opportunity to do so.

Retaining this transition period recognizes that complying with immigration requirements after an unexpected job loss involves practical steps that cannot always be completed immediately.

DHS should assess these consequences before removing the protection.

The proposal identifies reducing administrative burden as a justification for eliminating the grace period. I urge DHS to weigh that asserted benefit against the potential costs of increased employer pressure, reduced reporting of workplace misconduct, disruption to families, and diminished worker mobility.

In particular, DHS should examine how the proposed change would affect workers’ willingness to report mistreatment to human resources, labor enforcement agencies, or other appropriate authorities, and how those effects could influence conditions for U.S. workers.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed elimination of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days. Preserving a reasonable transition period supports orderly compliance with immigration requirements, reduces opportunities for employer coercion, and helps protect fair workplace standards for all workers in the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the removal of the grace period and urges DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ramakrishnan Arumugam Reddiar
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their dependents under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Many skilled professionals have dedicated several years of their lives contributing to the growth of the U.S. economy.

Unexpected layoffs and employment terminations can happen due to business restructuring, layoffs, termination, economic conditions, or circumstances beyond an employee’s control.

Removing this protection would create unnecessary stress, uncertainty, and financial hardship for thousands of skilled workers and their families.

H-1B workers have families, children attending American schools, homes, financial commitments, and established communities.

Children should not have their education and future disrupted because of circumstances beyond their parents’ control.

The existing grace period does not authorize unauthorized employment; it simply provides reasonable time to maintain immigration compliance and explore available options.

The United States should focus on retaining skilled international talent rather than forcing experienced professionals to leave unnecessarily.

I respectfully request DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period to protect workers, families, and American businesses.
comments.reason: The commenter argues for retaining the grace period and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: This rule should not be changed. People on H1 B visas have kids who go to school, own property and need time to work around finances and other issues before going back to the country of origin. 60 day grace period is a reasonable amount of time to work through things in case of loss of employment

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Akash Kamalesh Rana
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period. I sincerely urge DHS and USCIS to reconsider this proposal and recognize the devastating impact it could have on legal immigrants and their families.

This issue is deeply personal to me because both my wife and I have experienced unexpected layoffs.

I was previously laid off from my job while on an H-1B visa. I went through the incredibly stressful process of searching for a new employer while worrying about my immigration status and future in the United States. I was fortunate enough to have my H-1B transfer completed on the 60th day of my grace period.

Had this grace period not existed, I might not have been able to remain in the country and continue my career here. That experience taught me just how important those 60 days are. Even with the grace period, I barely made it.

More recently, my wife's position was eliminated in May, and she has been actively searching for employment since then. Once again, our family is experiencing the uncertainty that comes with an unexpected job loss.

We have worked hard to build our lives and careers in the United States. We contribute to the economy, pay taxes, follow immigration laws, and consider this country our home.

A layoff is not a choice an employee makes. Yet eliminating the grace period would effectively punish workers and their families for circumstances entirely outside their control.

Finding a new job is not something that happens overnight. It takes time to apply, interview, receive an offer, complete background checks, and navigate immigration paperwork. Even 60 days is an extremely short window to accomplish all of this.

Without the grace period, families like ours could face the possibility of having to uproot our lives and leave the country almost immediately after an unexpected layoff. The emotional and financial consequences would be enormous.

The 60-day grace period is not a special privilege. It is a reasonable and necessary safeguard that gives hardworking individuals a fair chance to recover from an unexpected setback.

I respectfully ask DHS and USCIS to consider the human impact of this proposal.

I am living proof that the 60-day grace period works. It gave me the opportunity to find another employer, maintain my immigration status, and continue contributing to this country. Without it, my life could have taken a completely different direction.

Please do not take away this critical protection from other families who may find themselves in the same situation.

If anything, the grace period should be extended to reflect the realities of today's job market, not eliminated.

We are not asking for special treatment. We are simply asking for a fair chance to navigate an unexpected job loss without the immediate fear of losing the lives we have spent years building.

I sincerely urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period harms workers and families facing unexpected layoffs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I request DHS and USCIS to retain the current 60 day grace period for alien workers who could unexpectedly lose employment.

This is a reasonable and limited safeguard.it is the right thing to give some time to these legal visa holders who trusted this country and came to work here legally. It does not authorize unauthorized work or guarantee continued stay. It simply gives affected workers a short period to find another qualifying employer or wrap up thier stuff and prepare to leave the United States in an orderly manner. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Losing a job can happen suddenly, often with little or no advance notice. Employees should not be forced to immediately leave the country because of circumstances beyond their control.

I urge USCIS to consider the following:

1. Family Stability: Many H-1B workers have lived legally in the U.S. for 10–20 years, raising families, buying homes, and building their lives here. Relocating an entire family immediately is simply not practical.
2. Children’s Education: Sudden relocation can disrupt children’s schooling, especially for children who were born or raised in the United States.
3. Finding New Employment: The U.S. hiring process involves multiple interviews, background checks, and immigration paperwork. Even 60 days can be challenging when searching for a new job.
4. Financial Responsibilities: Workers have mortgages, car loans, leases, and other financial commitments that cannot be resolved overnight.
5. Long Green Card Backlogs: Many H-1B workers have approved green card petitions but have waited years for permanent residency due to visa backlogs. They should not face immediate displacement after an unexpected layoff.
6. Impact on U.S. Businesses: Eliminating the grace period could cause American employers to lose experienced, skilled professionals who could otherwise transfer to another company.
7. Lawful Immigration: The existing grace period is temporary, not an indefinite extension of immigration status. It allows workers to find lawful alternatives or arrange an orderly departure.

The 60-day grace period is not a privilege being abused; it is an essential safety net for hardworking, law-abiding families.

Losing employment is already stressful. Adding the immediate threat of uprooting an entire family creates unnecessary hardship.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and consider the real-life impact on families who have contributed to the United States for many years.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the grace period, citing family stability, children's education, and job search challenges.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I moved to the US in June 2025, and as a 37-year-old single, child-free woman with no family to rely on, establishing a life here has been a significant undertaking. The prospect of suddenly finding myself without a job and being required to leave the country immediately is stressful enough. Not everyone owns a home or has family they can live with while finding a new job, securing somewhere to live and arranging transport back in their home country. These are not things that can realistically be organised overnight, particularly when returning to a country where you may no longer have an established life or support network.

The thought of dismantling the life I’ve worked so hard to build here would be heartbreaking. To then be expected to start again in my home country within hours is an enormous and unreasonable burden.

For many of us, the US has become more than a temporary place of employment. We are building lives, establishing communities and making meaningful contributions to the country and cities we have chosen to call home.

I appreciate that immigration policies may need to evolve. However, proposed changes must consider the real circumstances of those they affect. I would be grateful for a reasonable transition period to give individuals dignity, time and flexibility to make alternative arrangements without having their lives turned upside down overnight.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Marissa  Nicol
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose elimination of the 60-day grace period for highly skilled nonimmigrant visa holders under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). This grace period was instituted a decade ago for good reason and should remain.



I personally know someone who has an H-1B visa; he is a highly skilled and valued employee of a University who contributes to the University’s mission by helping farmers and rural communities. His situation is not unique.



The 60-day grace period is a sensible approach to real life circumstances. When someone loses their job through no fault of their own, they get 60 days to find a new sponsor, change jobs within the organization or get their affairs in order prior to leaving the country. Elimination of the grace period would turn every termination notice into an instant deportation order. This is not reform. It is punishment for the crime of losing a job.



Eliminating the grace period punishes employees for decisions made by their employer. These visa holders do not choose to be laid off, yet this change would require them to leave immediately if they are laid off. These workers have homes, families, schools their children attend, connections in their community. You cannot reasonably expect someone to leave those things overnight.



If these workers have to leave immediately upon losing their job, you will be harming landlords and banks who will be left with unpaid rent, broken leases and unpaid mortgages. You will be harming children who are suddenly yanked from their schools and their friends. You will be harming organizations where these workers volunteer and contribute their time and talent.



Eliminating this rule would create uncertainty for businesses and organizations that spend years sponsoring, training and retaining H-1B talent. If one of their workers loses their job due to a reorganization, there is no way for the organization to transfer them to another position in a reasonable timeframe. This does not help the U.S., it weakens our competitive edge by harming businesses and organizations that rely on these talented workers.



Elimination of the grace period does not recognize the realities of finding a new job in a specialized field if someone is laid off. This process involves interviews, background checks, internal reviews and time. Eliminating the grace period would make an unexpected layoff an immigration crisis.



Removing the grace period does not open jobs for Americans, it simply removes the small window of time that these talented workers have to find a new job if their current one no longer exists. This fear and uncertainty will force talented professionals out of the organizations that need them, harming both talented workers and the organizations that employ them.



In short, elimination of the grace period is cruel, reckless and causes more harm than good. Please retain the 60-day grace period.

Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security Officials,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety and preserve the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

The current grace period is an essential safeguard for law-abiding, highly skilled foreign professionals who contribute to the American economy, pay taxes, support American businesses, and build their lives and families in the United States.

1. Job Loss Is Often Beyond an Employee's Control

Layoffs, company restructuring, budget cuts, and economic downturns can affect even the most qualified and dedicated employees. Eliminating the grace period would impose severe immigration consequences on individuals who lose employment through no fault of their own.

Workers should not face the prospect of immediately leaving the country simply because their employer unexpectedly terminates their position.

2. Sixty Days Is Already a Very Limited Timeframe

Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an employment-based visa involves interviews, background checks, legal documentation, and immigration filings. Even 60 days can be insufficient to complete these steps.

Removing this limited transition period would make it significantly harder for qualified workers to secure new employment and maintain lawful immigration status.

3. Serious Consequences for Families and Children

Many affected workers have spouses and children who have established their lives in the United States. Children attend American schools, families maintain housing commitments, and households have financial obligations.

Requiring families to leave the United States immediately after an unexpected job loss could disrupt children's education, create financial hardship, and force families into difficult decisions without reasonable time to make arrangements.

Immigration policy should recognize these practical and humanitarian consequences.

4. Negative Consequences for American Businesses and Economic Competitiveness

American employers invest substantial time and resources in recruiting international talent. The existing grace period allows skilled workers to transition between employers without unnecessary disruption.

Eliminating this flexibility could cause American businesses to lose access to experienced professionals already living in the country, increase recruitment difficulties, and discourage international talent from pursuing long-term careers in the United States.

Maintaining a reasonable transition period benefits both American employers and the workers they hire.

5. Administrative Efficiency Should Not Come at the Expense of Fairness

DHS identifies administrative burden and the relationship between employment and immigration status as reasons for the proposed change. However, the agency should consider whether those objectives can be achieved through less disruptive alternatives.

The existing grace period is discretionary, limited in duration, and does not provide indefinite immigration status or unrestricted employment authorization.

DHS should provide clear evidence that eliminating this protection would produce benefits sufficient to outweigh the resulting economic, administrative, and humanitarian consequences.

6. Preserve Stability and Predictability in the Immigration System

Employment-based visa holders are expected to comply with immigration laws, maintain valid status, and follow complex regulatory requirements. They should also have access to reasonable and predictable procedures when circumstances change unexpectedly.

The 60-day grace period helps provide that stability without removing DHS's authority to enforce immigration requirements.

Conclusion and Request

I respectfully request that DHS:

Withdraw the proposed rule eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period.

Retain the existing protections under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Fully consider the impact on workers, employers, spouses, and children.

Evaluate less restrictive alternatives to address administrative concerns without imposing disproportionate hardship.

Losing a job should not automatically mean losing the ability to remain in the country without a reasonable transition period.

The United States benefits from an immigration system that balances lawful enforcement with fairness, economic stability, and family well-being.

I strongly urge USCIS and DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering this public comment.

Strong Opposition to the Proposed Rule Change Regarding the H-1B 60-Day Grace Period
I am writing in strong opposition to the proposed rule change affecting the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders.
For the past ten years, I have lived and worked in the United States on an H-1B visa at the direct invitation of American companies. While I recognize that the H-1B is a temporary visa rather than a birthright, it is legally defined as a "dual-intent" visa that places skilled workers on a lawful, Congressionally approved path toward permanent residency. Because the United States creates that legitimate expectation of long-term stability, those who abide by the rules build deep, meaningful lives here.
The relationship between H-1B workers and the United States is fundamentally mutually beneficial. Many of America’s most iconic companies would not exist today without immigrant talent, and several of the top CEOs driving the U.S. economy originally came here through this exact system, helping make this country what it is today. To maintain its global leadership, America should focus on fostering growth rather than blindly pushing out highly skilled workers before an equivalent domestic talent pool has been built to replace them. If the policy goal is to manage workforce numbers, the solution is to adjust the volume of new incoming visas—not to pull the rug out from under vetted, tax-paying professionals who are already integrated into American communities and industries.
Furthermore, eliminating or restricting the 60-day grace period is logistically impossible and deeply inhumane. After a decade of contributing to this country, you cannot simply keep your bags packed and uproot a life on a one-day notice. People have mortgages, car leases, financial obligations, and deep community ties. Most importantly, we have families; my child is a U.S.-born American citizen enrolled in school who deserves stability in his own country. A complex life built over ten years cannot be snapped out of existence overnight.
Debating whether to allow an adjustment of status or a change of visa category during a transition is a separate policy matter. However, stripping away the fundamental buffer of a 60-day grace period forces law-abiding families into immediate crisis. Even when a visa holder’s time in the United States comes to an end, the transition must be handled with basic human dignity and practical grace—which is the exact purpose the 60-day period serves.
I urge you to reject this proposed change and preserve the 60-day grace period, which provides essential stability for American businesses, skilled workers, and our U.S. citizen children.

A pending adjustment application does not, by itself, protect me: work authorization renewals can take months, a request for evidence can arrive at any time, and any gap or technical problem leaves me with no lawful status to fall back on.

That is not an edge case. Hundreds of thousands of workers are waiting in the employment-based backlog, many of them for years, and every one of them depends on the grace period as the bridge between one sponsor and the next. Eliminating it turns a single employer restructuring decision into the destruction of a lawful immigration case that the government itself invited the worker to file.

This rule would not create a single American job. My position would be eliminated, not refilled, and the only thing destroyed would be years of lawful compliance. The grace period is already discretionary: DHS can deny it to anyone who abuses it. Please keep that case-by-case tool and withdraw this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for H-1B, H-1B1, E-1, E-2, E-3, L-1, O-1 and TN workers and their dependents.

DHS created this grace period in 2017. It recognized that skilled workers often lose their jobs suddenly, through layoffs, restructurings or project cancellations, for reasons that have nothing to do with them. The grace period gives these workers a short window to find a new sponsoring employer, change status or leave the country in an orderly way. Taking it away would bring back the problem it was created to fix.

It punishes people for being laid off. Without the grace period, a worker who loses a job through no fault of their own would immediately fall out of status. Many have spent years in the U.S. with homes, leases, children in school and pending green card cases. Making them leave right away, or putting them in a position where they might accrue unlawful presence, is out of proportion to anything they did.
It hurts U.S. employers and the economy. Industries such as life sciences, healthcare, technology and consulting depend on these workers. The grace period lets employers hire talent that is already in the U.S. and has already been vetted. Without it, those workers would be forced to leave the country, and employers would face longer hiring cycles, higher costs and lost productivity.
It will not reduce the burden on the agency. DHS says the change would cut adjudication burdens. In practice, workers who cannot move to a new employer while staying in the U.S. will turn to emergency change-of-status filings, B-2 extensions, consular processing and requests for relief. That means more filings for USCIS and the State Department, not fewer.
It makes the U.S. less competitive. Other countries actively recruit skilled workers and give them reasonable time to change jobs. Making U.S. status this fragile will push talent and investment elsewhere.
The current rule already protects program integrity. The grace period is discretionary, capped at 60 days or the end of the authorized validity period (whichever comes first), and available only once per authorized validity period. It does not authorize employment. DHS has not shown evidence of abuse that would justify removing it outright instead of applying the existing limits.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and keep the grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

This artificial constraint does not just penalize visa holders navigating complex, multi-week hiring and petition timelines; it actively hurts U.S. workers by distorting fair wage floors, incentivizing captive-workforce labor models, and preventing domestic firms from competing on a level, merit-based playing field. Codified in 2016 to maintain healthy labor market flexibility and economic stability, the 60-day buffer ensures competitive parity across industries; eliminating it weakens wage growth, damages employer agility, and undermines the broader American workforce.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule in DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 and ask DHS to withdraw it.
I have lived in the United States since 2009 and have been on H-1B since 2011. I work as a Regulatory Affairs Director in the medical technology industry in Massachusetts. I have had an approved I-140 since 2014 and have waited more than 12 years in the green card backlog. I live here with my wife — who is on her own visa and in the same position — and our three young children, ages 6, 4 and 1, who are U.S. citizens and have only ever lived in the United States. We own our home and have a mortgage of $6,000 a month, and our older child is in school here.
If my employment ended on a Friday, this rule would treat my whole family as out of status by Saturday. We could not sell our home, withdraw our child from school, arrange international travel for a family of four, or find a new employer and have a new petition filed in one day. In my experience, transitioning to a new job takes anywhere from a few weeks to months on average. The 60-day grace period, in place since January 2017, is what makes H-1B portability under INA § 214(n) work in practice, and workers and employers have reasonably relied on it for nearly a decade.
Congress created H-1B portability under INA § 214(n) so an eligible worker can begin working for a new employer when a qualifying petition is filed, and job-change flexibility for employment-based green card applicants under INA § 204(j). The grace period is what makes portability work in practice: it gives a worker time to find a new employer, obtain a certified Labor Condition Application, and have a new petition filed without first leaving the country. Without it, a worker ready to be hired by another U.S. company could be forced to depart and seek readmission instead.
In my field — regulatory affairs for medical technology — roles are specialized and hiring cycles are measured in weeks to months, not days. In my experience, transitioning to a new job takes at least 90 days on average. Even with a prompt job offer, the Labor Condition Application and petition filing steps alone take time beyond a worker’s control. Without the grace period, that timeline makes portability unusable in practice.
In footnote 19 (91 Fed. Reg. at 57,812 n.19), DHS proposes removing the reference to the 60-day grace period from 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) and calls it a “technical revision.” It is not merely technical. Workers with approved I-140 petitions can currently apply during the grace period for a compelling circumstances Employment Authorization Document (EAD) if they meet the other requirements. DHS should retain this protection regardless of what it decides on the grace period itself, and should analyze its effects separately rather than in a footnote. I have had an approved I-140 since 2014 and have waited more than 12 years in the backlog. If I lost my job, a compelling circumstances Employment Authorization Document is one of the few safety nets that could allow my family to remain lawfully while facing serious hardship, rather than being forced to leave immediately. Removing access to it during the grace period would remove that protection precisely when it is needed most.
The proposal makes the end date of employment immediately consequential, yet that date is not always clear: workers may receive advance notice, remain on payroll during a notice period, receive severance, be placed on furlough, or face disputes about their final day. A disagreement about that date could determine whether a worker maintained status or a later filing was timely. DHS should clearly define cessation of employment and address paid notice periods, furloughs, and similar arrangements before imposing immediate consequences. The current grace period reduces the harm from that uncertainty.
The grace period gives a worker some protection against becoming immediately dependent on an employer’s decisions. Without it, a worker who reports unpaid wages, discrimination, harassment, or unsafe working conditions risks immediate loss of status if the employer retaliates by terminating employment.
DHS has acknowledged it did not quantify the costs of this rule — lost wages, housing losses, and international relocation. For my family, a forced departure would mean selling our home, both cars, and our household belongings on a rushed basis — upwards of tens of thousands of dollars just to hire people to handle that wind-down, plus substantial losses from untimely sales, on top of a $6,000 monthly mortgage, lost wages, and relocation costs. DHS could also address its administrative concern more narrowly, for example by revising Forms I-129 and I-539 so applicants identify reliance on the grace period, rather than eliminating the period entirely.
Thank you for considering my comment.
“Anonymous” — H-1B Regulatory Affairs Director in medical technology, Massachusetts
comments.reason: The commenter argues against removing the grace period because it harms families and makes job transitions impossible.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). A layoff is an employer’s decision, not evidence that a worker or their family has done anything wrong. Yet this proposal would turn the loss of a job into an immediate immigration crisis for people who have followed the rules and built their lives in the United States.

Sixty days is not a guarantee of a new job, and it does not authorize someone to keep working without permission. It is a limited opportunity to interview, secure a qualifying offer, and have the necessary petition or application filed. Removing that window would make an ordinary job transition far harder, especially when a new employer must evaluate the candidate and prepare an immigration filing. It would also force spouses and children to face upheaval because of a layoff they could not control.

This is a poor signal to the talent the United States wants to attract. An exceptional engineer, researcher, physician, or entrepreneur deciding where to build a career will consider not only the opportunity on offer, but whether one unexpected layoff could destabilize their entire family. Employers would lose the chance to hire skilled people already living here, while workers would have less freedom to move to the job where they can contribute most.

DHS should not retain but increase the grace period to 180 days. If the agency has concerns about how it is administered, it should address those concerns directly rather than eliminate the transition period altogether. A country competing for extraordinary talent should not make a routine layoff a reason for that talent to leave.

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

Since then, I have held leadership roles in software companies, technology businesses, and AI-native organizations. My experience has taught me something important: **High-skilled immigrants do not simply fill American jobs. They help create them.**

Throughout my career, I have worked with American engineers, recruiters, executive assistants, operations leaders, and business professionals. I have witnessed how skilled immigrants bring specialized expertise, entrepreneurial energy, and fresh perspectives that help American companies innovate, grow, and create employment opportunities.

Immigration generates economic activity far beyond the individual worker.

When companies grow, they hire recruiters, engineers, salespeople, executives, and support staff. Immigrant families rent and purchase homes, buy goods and services, pay taxes, and support local businesses. Their economic participation benefits industries including real estate, banking, insurance, retail, transportation, education, legal services, and logistics.

The impact is especially visible in recruitment. Employment mobility generates substantial economic activity across staffing agencies, executive search firms, HR technology companies, and professional services.

Restricting the ability of skilled workers to transition between employers risks reducing this activity, making hiring more difficult and weakening the broader ecosystem that supports American employment.

Layoffs often occur because of corporate restructuring, economic cycles, or business decisions completely outside an employee's control. Removing the 60-day grace period could transform an unexpected job loss into an immediate immigration crisis.

It could also result in the departure of experienced professionals whom American companies have spent years recruiting, training, and developing.

These workers could otherwise join another American company, help grow an existing business, or establish a new enterprise that creates additional American jobs.

The consequences also extend to families.

My wife works in education, directly supporting American students and communities. Like many immigrant households, our family contributes across multiple sectors of American society.

Eliminating the grace period creates unnecessary instability for families with children in American schools, spouses working in local communities, and established financial obligations.

I recognize the importance of immigration compliance and effective administration. However, reducing administrative burden should not come at the expense of broader economic opportunity.

comments.commentText:
I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their dependents.

For many skilled professionals, moving to the United States is not simply an employment decision. It is a major family decision involving relocation, financial commitments, housing, children’s education, and building a new life in a different country. Many families move to the United States with the hope of achieving the American dream and contributing their professional skills to the country.

If an individual’s employment unexpectedly ends, finding another employer, completing the necessary immigration procedures, arranging a transfer, or making the difficult decision to relocate the entire family back to their home country cannot realistically happen overnight.

The 60-day grace period provides an essential transition window during an already stressful and uncertain time. It gives employees a reasonable opportunity to explore new employment, maintain their family’s stability, and make informed decisions about their future.

Eliminating this period could also create an imbalance in the employer-employee relationship. Employees who have relocated internationally with their families may feel pressured to remain with their existing employer, even when better professional opportunities exist or their employment circumstances are no longer favorable, simply because they do not have sufficient time to transition.

I understand that DHS may have concerns about the discretionary nature and administration of this grace period. However, completely eliminating it may create disproportionate hardship for workers and their families.

I strongly encourage DHS to consider retaining the 60-day grace period or, at a minimum, reducing it to 30 or 45 days rather than eliminating it entirely. Another option would be to retain the discretionary provision while allowing reasonable flexibility based on individual circumstances.

A reasonable transition period is important not only for the employee but also for their spouse and children, who are equally affected by an unexpected employment termination.

I respectfully request that DHS consider the real-life circumstances of immigrant families before finalizing this proposal. Thank you for considering the perspectives of affected workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their families.

This proposal is not merely an administrative change. It has the potential to uproot families, disrupt children's lives, undermine American businesses, and weaken the principles of fairness, opportunity, and family stability that have long been central to the American identity.

1. Losing a job should not mean losing one's entire life overnight.

A job loss is already a devastating event for many families. It brings financial uncertainty, emotional distress, and the difficult task of finding new employment. For workers on visas such as the H-1B, the consequences are even greater because their family's ability to remain in the country is tied to their employment.

The current 60-day grace period offers a modest opportunity to find another employer, arrange a lawful change of status, or make necessary arrangements. It does not grant permanent residence, nor does it authorize unrestricted employment. It simply provides a reasonable measure of stability during an unexpected transition.

Eliminating even this limited protection would turn an ordinary employment setback into a potential family crisis.

2. Families and children are not disposable consequences of employment decisions.

Many employment-based immigrants have lived in the United States for years, sometimes decades. They have purchased homes, paid taxes, raised children, volunteered, supported local businesses, and become deeply integrated into their communities.

Their children attend American schools, form friendships, participate in sports and community activities, and consider America their home. Some are American citizens by birth.

Under this proposal, a parent's unexpected job loss could force an entire family into an immediate immigration crisis. Children could face abrupt school disruption, separation from friends, and the loss of the only home they have ever known. Families could be forced to abandon established lives while simultaneously coping with unemployment.

The proposed rule's Family Assessment concludes that its impact on family well-being would be negligible. I respectfully challenge that conclusion. The practical and emotional consequences of sudden displacement cannot reasonably be described as negligible.

3. America should not punish lawful participation and long-term contribution.

Employment-based immigrants come to the United States through legal processes, comply with demanding immigration requirements, and contribute their skills and labor to American businesses.

Many have invested the most productive years of their lives in this country while waiting through lengthy employment-based green card backlogs. They have followed the rules, built careers, and made long-term commitments to their communities.

Yet this proposal would make their ability to remain in the country even more precarious, regardless of their years of lawful residence, tax contributions, or family responsibilities.

A system that expects people to contribute to American society for decades while denying them even a short period to recover from unexpected unemployment risks undermining public confidence in the fairness and predictability of that system.

4. The deeper concern is what this policy says about American values.

The United States has long drawn strength from people who come here seeking opportunity, work diligently, raise families, and contribute to the communities around them.

The American promise has never been simply about employment or economic productivity. It is also about dignity, fairness, responsibility, family, and the opportunity to build a better future through hard work.

When a person can lose their job through circumstances beyond their control and immediately face the prospect of uprooting their spouse and children, we must ask whether our policies reflect those values.

The strength of America's social fabric lies in stable families, strong communities, mutual trust, and the belief that people who follow the rules will be treated with basic fairness.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period. At a minimum, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the effects on children, families, employers, and long-term lawful residents, and consider alternatives that preserve reasonable transition protections.

Sixty days is not an unreasonable privilege. It is a modest, humane accommodation that recognizes that workers are also parents, spouses, neighbors, homeowners, and members of communities.

America can maintain strong immigration laws without abandoning compassion, proportionality, and common sense.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to eliminating the grace period, citing family disruption and hardship.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

This comment is in opposition to the proposed rule that seeks to eliminate the discretionary up-to-60-day grace period currently available to certain employment-based nonimmigrants following the end of their qualifying employment. I believe that this rule would create substantial harms that significantly outweigh any claimed administrative benefits.

Since the grace period was instituted in 2017, employers, employees, educational institutions, attorneys, and families have developed considerable reliance interests around the availability of the grace period, which offers a reasonable period of time for changes in employment to be made. The proposed rule offers insufficient evidence that the existing system has caused widespread abuse, fraud, security concerns, or noteworthy harm to the public interest. Without such evidence, completely eliminating a longstanding policy that has provided stability and flexibility to both workers and employers is unwarranted and will lead to more harm than good. It will also create additional administrative burden for DHS and other government agencies in terms of NTAs, immigration hearings, etc., which is counter to DHS’s goal of reducing such work.

More specifically, this proposed rule fails to account for such workers as medical residents and fellows on H-1B status who transition from one employing entity to another as they finish one training program and begin another to continue their long-term goal of becoming fully qualified to provide patient care in the U.S., undoubtedly a worthy endeavor that benefits the American public. In such situations, these workers may have a brief gap in employment due to fixed start and end dates of these training programs which are not able to be adjusted. The elimination of the grace period would have an outsized impact on these workers and potentially rob our country of their dedicated service to the medical profession.

If DHS believes that modifications to the grace period are necessary, it should consider less disruptive alternatives that will still address their concerns, such as:
•Retaining the 60-day grace period, while improving guidance regarding eligibility and documentation requirements.
•Retaining the 60-day grace period, while establishing enhanced reporting mechanisms following employment termination.
•Shortening the 60-day grace period only if evidence demonstrates a specific problem requiring correction.
•Preserving the grace period for workers with pending adjustment-of-status applications and pending/approved immigrant petitions.

In summary, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the current up-to-60-day discretionary grace period for eligible nonimmigrant workers and their dependents. The existing policy promotes labor market flexibility, supports American employers, protects families from unnecessary hardship, and allows aspiring lawful immigrants a reasonable opportunity to pursue continued compliance with U.S. immigration laws. The benefits of the current rule substantially outweigh the administrative considerations cited in the proposed rule.

Thank you for your consideration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Opposition to the Proposed Rule Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period for Nonimmigrant Workers

We are writing to oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule eliminating the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers who lose their employment. We speak for the many nonimmigrant workers and families in the same position across the United States — people who work lawfully, live in our communities, own or rent our homes, and send our children to local schools. This rule would directly threaten our families' stability.

The 60-day grace period is already the minimum workable window, not a luxury. Finding a new employer willing to sponsor a transfer, completing interviews, and having a new petition prepared and filed realistically takes weeks. Sixty days is barely enough. Eliminating it would leave workers with virtually no time to do any of this lawfully.

A grace period of zero days leaves no lawful path in practice. Workers who are laid off through no fault of our own would have no lawful way to remain in the United States while seeking new sponsored employment, and would instead face immediate departure — abandoning our homes, our mortgages, and our children's school year. A system that gives law-abiding workers no lawful option to stay while we pursue a new petition is not an orderly system.

The harm extends beyond the worker. Families on dependent visas are affected in the same way. American employers lose trained, experienced employees overnight with no transition. Communities lose neighbors, and the housing market and local economy absorb sudden, forced departures. None of this serves the public interest.

For our children, the harm would come in a single day. Most of our children are U.S. citizens — born here, and many have never lived anywhere else. If we had to leave with no grace period, those American citizen children would in effect be forced to leave the country they were born in, or face separation from a parent who must depart. Either way, their lives would change overnight: pulled out of school in the middle of the year, taken from their teachers, friends, and daily routines, with no time to say goodbye, transfer school records, or plan for what comes next. A child's schooling, friendships, and sense of stability should not end in a day because a parent was laid off through no fault of their own.

The current grace period supports lawful compliance. It gives workers a defined, lawful window to find a new sponsor, have a petition filed, change status through lawful channels, or prepare an orderly departure. DHS has not shown that the grace period is being abused, nor that eliminating it would solve any identified problem. Retaining it serves workers, families, and employers alike, and it serves the orderly administration of the immigration system.

We respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period, which is a modest and necessary protection for workers, families, and employers alike.

Sincerely,
Concerned nonimmigrant workers and their families

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing about the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period (Docket USCIS-2026-0364). I want to explain what this looks like inside a real home.
I came to the United States in 2011 on a work visa. I have lived here for more than a decade and built my life here. I have two children, ages 6 and 12, who were born here and are American citizens. They know one country, one school, one set of friends. My family bought a house, and every month we pay the mortgage. I pay my taxes and have never taken anything I wasn’t entitled to. I have followed every rule.
Under this proposal, my status would end the day after my job does. Not 60 days, not 30 days, not one week. The next day. A layoff, a company closing, a bad manager, a restructuring I had no part in, and by the following morning I would be out of status and expected to leave.
Please think about what that day looks like. My 12-year-old is in the middle of the school year. My 6-year-old is just learning to read. They are U.S. citizens, and their lives would be thrown into chaos because of a decision made in someone else’s office. I would have to tell them that we may have to leave the only home they have ever known, or that I might have to go while they stay. No parent should have to have that conversation with a child on a day’s notice.
And the house. You cannot sell a house in a day. The mortgage is due whether or not I have a paycheck. The notice itself acknowledges (Section IV.D) that people in my position have bought homes, paid taxes, and invested in their communities, and then concludes the harm is outweighed. It treats this as a footnote. For us it is everything we have worked for.
The grace period exists for exactly this. Sixty days is not a free pass. It is time to find a new employer, file the paperwork, and arrange an orderly transition while keeping a roof over the heads of citizen children. The notice’s own data show that thousands of people each year use that window to land new jobs and stay productive. Those are workers employers wanted to hire.
I was also troubled by the Family Assessment (Section V.F), which calls the impact on families “negligible” and “incidental.” I do not see how anyone could say that about a rule that can end a family’s income, housing stability, and children’s schooling at once. The notice does not mention U.S. citizen children at all. They are not “aliens,” but they will bear the consequences more than anyone. The estimate of costs also excludes dependents entirely, calling the data “not salient enough.” Children are not a data problem. They are the people this rule will hurt most.
The notice says the goal is to reduce administrative burden. But the burden of this rule falls on families, not on the agency. The government would save some adjudication time, while the cost lands on children who did nothing except be born into a family that played by the rules.
I am not asking DHS to ignore the law. I am asking for a reasonable, humane process: a grace period that is clear, predictable, and long enough for a family to protect its children while finding a path forward. If DHS has concerns about fraud or misuse, address those directly with clear exceptions instead of removing the protection for everyone.
Please withdraw this proposal, or at least keep a defined grace period for families with U.S. citizen children and homes here. Behind the numbers in this notice are real children, and their stability should count.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by A S
comments.commentText:
I support eliminating the 60-day grace period currently afforded to H-1B nonimmigrants following the termination of their employment. I also believe the Department should address the broader problem of employers potentially exploiting employment-based immigration programs at the expense of American workers.

The H-1B program is intended to address legitimate employer demand for specialized talent. However, the existing 60-day grace period creates opportunities for individuals to remain in the United States after their employment has ended, including by attempting to change to B-1/B-2 visitor status while searching for another employer willing to sponsor them.

Visitor classifications are not intended to serve as an alternative employment-based immigration pathway. Although individuals may have certain permissible activities while in visitor status, the government should carefully scrutinize attempts to use visitor status as a mechanism for extending residence primarily to pursue employment opportunities. Eliminating the automatic 60-day grace period would reinforce the temporary nature of H-1B employment and discourage the use of alternative immigration classifications to extend an otherwise terminated employment-based stay.

Equally important, the Department should examine potential abuse by employers themselves.

There is a troubling disconnect when large corporations simultaneously conduct substantial layoffs, offer voluntary employee exit programs, reduce their domestic workforce, and continue asserting that they cannot find sufficient qualified American workers to justify employing foreign workers through H-1B and PERM sponsorship.

For example, Microsoft has publicly discussed workforce restructuring and voluntary exit opportunities while continuing to maintain that it needs access to foreign talent. This raises legitimate questions about how employers determine that a shortage of qualified U.S. workers exists when they are simultaneously encouraging existing employees to leave.

The PERM labor certification process exists to protect U.S. workers by requiring employers to demonstrate that sufficient qualified and available American workers cannot be found for the relevant position. It should not become a procedural mechanism through which companies can continually recruit foreign workers while reducing their existing American workforce.

The Department should investigate whether employers are using PERM applications to fill genuine labor shortages or whether some are strategically structuring recruitment activities to facilitate immigration sponsorship despite having qualified American workers available. Particular scrutiny should be given to employers conducting layoffs, voluntary separation programs, or workforce reductions while simultaneously pursuing labor certifications for comparable positions.

The government should not evaluate immigration compliance solely by examining whether an employer has technically completed the required recruitment steps. It should also consider the broader employment circumstances, including workforce reductions, the availability of qualified domestic employees, and whether the employer's claims of labor shortages are consistent with its actual hiring and staffing decisions.

There must be accountability on both sides of the employment-based immigration system. Foreign workers should not be permitted to use successive immigration classifications to circumvent the temporary nature of their authorized employment, and employers should not be permitted to exploit immigration sponsorship programs while displacing or unnecessarily eliminating opportunities for American workers.

I encourage the Department to eliminate the automatic 60-day H-1B grace period and strengthen oversight of employer compliance with H-1B and PERM requirements. Protecting the integrity of employment-based immigration programs requires ensuring that they serve their intended purpose rather than becoming mechanisms for employers to maintain access to foreign labor while disregarding the interests of the domestic workforce.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states support for eliminating the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jonathan Batis
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose DHS's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for eligible nonimmigrant workers. I strongly urge DHS to retain this important safeguard, which provides a reasonable balance between immigration enforcement and the realities of unexpected job loss.

1. Reasonable Time for Employment Transitions

Finding a new job, especially in specialized fields, requires interviews, background checks, employer approvals, and immigration processing. These steps often take several weeks. Eliminating the grace period would turn an unexpected layoff into an immediate immigration crisis, even for workers who have consistently followed the law.

2. Protecting Families and Children

Many nonimmigrant workers have built their lives in the United States, paying taxes, purchasing homes, and raising children in American schools. Sudden job loss is already difficult. Removing the grace period would create additional uncertainty around housing, education, healthcare, and family stability. Families with young children or dependents requiring ongoing medical care would be particularly vulnerable.

3. Supporting American Businesses

U.S. employers benefit from retaining experienced, highly skilled professionals. Removing the grace period could disrupt recruitment, increase hiring uncertainty, and cause businesses to lose qualified talent. It could also make the United States less attractive to skilled workers considering long-term careers here.

4. Encouraging Fairness and Legal Compliance

Layoffs often result from restructuring or economic conditions beyond an employee's control. Workers who have maintained lawful status deserve a reasonable opportunity to find another employer, pursue an eligible change of status, or arrange an orderly departure. The current grace period is limited and discretionary; it does not authorize indefinite stay or unrestricted employment.

Conclusion

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period. Eliminating it would create unnecessary hardship for law-abiding workers, their families, and American employers without a clearly demonstrated benefit to immigration enforcement.

Maintaining this limited protection supports fairness, family stability, lawful compliance, and America's ability to attract and retain skilled talent.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Respectfully submitted,

A Nonimmigrant Professional and Concerned Member of the U.S. Workforce
