comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dennis Ma
comments.commentText:
I write as an individual to oppose the proposed rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364). The rule is justified as a burden reduction. On the mechanics of how the current provision actually operates, it would do the opposite: it eliminates a protection that costs the agency nothing to administer, and replaces it with new filings, new adjudications, and new enforcement cases that USCIS and the taxpayer will have to pay for.

Start with the present baseline. The grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) is self-executing. A worker whose employment ends files nothing, pays nothing, and consumes no officer time; status continues by operation of the regulation. There is no grace-period application in USCIS's inventory and no grace-period backlog. The burden DHS cites — that officers had to "consider" the provision's applicability in some 1.9 million filings since fiscal 2018 — is a threshold check performed inside petitions and applications that were filed for other reasons and will continue to be filed whether or not this rule is adopted. Eliminating the grace period does not eliminate a single one of those adjudications. It eliminates only the answer's simplicity.

What elimination creates is new work. A worker who is out of status the day after a layoff, but who has a realistic prospect of a new sponsor or a pending immigration benefit, will not simply vanish; he will file. Expect defensive change-of-status applications on Form I-539, compelling-circumstances employment authorization requests under 8 CFR 204.5(p), motions to reopen and reconsider on Form I-290B when filings go wrong, and a rising volume of expedite requests, service requests, and congressional inquiries from workers and employers trying to establish on which day employment "ceased" and status was lost. Every one of those items is a real adjudication consuming real officer hours at an agency whose backlogs are already measured in years. The proposed companion change to section 204.5(p)(1)(i), forcing the first compelling-circumstances request to be filed while the worker is still in status, accelerates still more filings into that channel. A rule cannot reduce adjudicative burden by converting a zero-touch regulatory provision into four fee-and-labor filing streams.

The costs USCIS does not absorb land on the taxpayer. USCIS is largely fee-funded; the immigration courts and ICE are not. Workers who would have found a new sponsor within 60 days, or departed in an orderly way at their own expense, instead become candidates for notices to appear, immigration court dockets that are already backlogged into the millions of cases, detention, and government-funded removal. Each case in that pipeline costs orders of magnitude more than the zero dollars the grace period costs today. The ledger loses on the revenue side as well: a worker pushed out of status stops paying the income and payroll taxes he paid while employed, and a worker who gives up and leaves takes with him the future filing fees and tax contributions of the remaining years of his authorized stay. Finally, this rule will be litigated, as the recent fixed-admission rule for students was — and there the government's defense has already consumed agency and Justice Department resources in a case where implementation is now enjoined nationwide. DHS should price its own litigation exposure into the burden analysis; the preamble does not.

The preamble's own figures show how thin the justification is. If only 3,795 beneficiaries are projected to lose income from this change, the affected population is small; if 1.9 million filings truly required grace-period consideration, the provision was functioning as a routine, low-friction part of adjudication. Either way, the arithmetic does not support repeal. It supports, at most, the narrower alternatives DHS declined to evaluate seriously, such as shortening the period or preserving it for workers with approved immigrant petitions whose reliance interests are deepest. Under Regents of the University of California v. DHS and Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm, an agency reversing a decade-old policy must assess reliance interests and consider significant alternatives; pointing to a burden the rule would increase rather than decrease is not a reasoned basis for repeal.

The grace period is one of the cheapest provisions in the immigration system precisely because it asks nothing of the government. Repealing it would not relieve USCIS or the taxpayer. It would bill both. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

Dennis Ma
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule, arguing it creates more bureaucratic work and harms workers.

comments.commentText: I worked for almost six years on a TN visa, and I believe the 60-day grace period is very beneficial for visa holders, as it frees us from abusive and corrupt employers. If this 60-day grace period to find another employer hadn't existed, I wouldn't have had the money to return to my country, which would have jeopardized my well-being and human rights. Thanks to the 60-day period, I was able to successfully change employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Robert Grey
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period.

DHS has not adequately explained how the proposed rule would interact with the statutory H-1B portability framework established by INA §214(n), 8 U.S.C. §1184(n).

Congress established H-1B portability to facilitate transitions between qualifying employers without requiring an otherwise eligible worker to remain indefinitely with a prior employer while a new petition is processed.

The proposed rule would substantially alter the circumstances in which an H-1B worker may transition between employers following an involuntary termination.

DHS states that the proposed rule would not eliminate statutory portability. However, merely stating that INA §214(n) remains unchanged does not resolve the practical and legal questions created by the proposed elimination of the grace period.

DHS must explain how the following situations would be treated:

1. An H-1B worker is involuntarily terminated while the previously approved petition remains valid.
2. A new employer files an H-1B petition after the termination but before the expiration of the worker's previously issued I-94.
3. The new employer files a petition after the worker has been considered to have failed to maintain H-1B status under the proposed rule.
4. The new employer requests an extension of stay or change of employer in connection with the new petition.
5. USCIS approves the petition but denies the requested extension of stay because of the prior employment termination.

DHS should identify the precise statutory and regulatory basis for determining whether each worker satisfies the applicable portability requirements.

The agency should not leave employers and workers to infer whether the proposed rule effectively narrows a statutory portability protection through a regulatory change that does not amend INA §214(n).

If DHS believes that the proposed rule does not affect portability, it should explain how an individual who is no longer considered to be maintaining H-1B status can nevertheless satisfy the applicable statutory requirements for portability.

If DHS believes that the proposed rule does affect portability, it must explain the statutory authority for that result and address whether the proposal conflicts with congressional objectives underlying INA §214(n).

This is not a minor technical issue. It directly affects the ability of U.S. employers to recruit qualified workers who have recently experienced involuntary employment termination.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposal. At a minimum, DHS must provide a detailed analysis of INA §214(n), clarify the treatment of pending and subsequently filed petitions, and ensure that the final rule does not undermine statutory portability protections.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Maria Bautista
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

DHS has not adequately addressed the fact that the existing 10-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(1) does not provide a meaningful substitute for the 60-day grace period when employment terminates before the expiration of an individual's authorized period of stay.

For example, an H-1B worker may have an approved petition and an unexpired I-94 authorizing admission for another two years. If the employer unexpectedly terminates the worker's employment because of a corporate restructuring or reduction in force, the proposed rule would eliminate the existing transition period even though the worker's previously authorized period of stay has not expired.

The 10-day provision does not solve this problem.

DHS must explain why a worker who loses employment involuntarily well before the expiration of the authorized period of stay should be treated as having no meaningful transition period, while the regulatory framework continues to recognize a separate 10-day period in other circumstances.

The agency should also explain why it believes that the existing regulatory framework cannot be improved through a shorter, clearly defined transition period rather than eliminating the protection entirely.

The distinction is particularly important because employment termination may occur without advance notice. Workers may need time to obtain termination documentation, contact immigration counsel, identify a new qualifying employer, prepare a petition, evaluate a change of status, or arrange departure.

DHS should not characterize the 10-day provision as an adequate alternative unless it explains how that provision applies to workers terminated during an otherwise unexpired period of authorized stay.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposal. Alternatively, DHS should preserve a meaningful transition period for individuals whose employment terminates before the expiration of their authorized period of stay.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, arguing the 10-day alternative is insufficient.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Don Krause
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed amendments to 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i).

DHS has not adequately evaluated the combined effect of eliminating the 60-day grace period and narrowing the regulatory circumstances relevant to eligibility for initial compelling circumstances employment authorization.

This issue is particularly significant for employment-based immigrant petition beneficiaries who have approved Form I-140 petitions but cannot yet file for adjustment of status because an immigrant visa number is unavailable.

These individuals may have spent years pursuing permanent residence through the employment-based immigration system. Their inability to file Form I-485 may result from statutory visa-number limitations and backlogs that are entirely outside their control.

If such an individual experiences involuntary employment termination, eliminating the grace period may substantially reduce the opportunity to pursue compelling circumstances employment authorization under the applicable regulatory requirements.

DHS must explain why individuals who have made substantial progress toward permanent residence should face a substantially more restrictive transition framework solely because their priority dates are not current.

The agency should separately evaluate:

1. Beneficiaries with approved I-140 petitions whose priority dates are not current.
2. Beneficiaries who are otherwise potentially eligible for compelling circumstances employment authorization.
3. Workers whose employment terminates before they can secure a new qualifying employer.
4. Workers whose ability to file Form I-485 is delayed by visa-number availability rather than any failure to comply with immigration law.
5. The effect of eliminating the existing grace-period reference in 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i).

DHS should also explain why it considers the resulting restrictions consistent with the purpose of the compelling circumstances employment authorization framework.

The agency should not disregard the fact that employment-based immigrant visa backlogs may prevent otherwise qualified beneficiaries from pursuing adjustment of status for extended periods.

A worker should not be forced into an unnecessarily severe immigration consequence because the statutory visa allocation system prevents the worker from immediately completing the permanent residence process.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed amendments. Alternatively, DHS should preserve an appropriate transition mechanism for qualifying employment-based immigrant petition beneficiaries and provide a separate, comprehensive analysis of the impact on compelling circumstances employment authorization.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, arguing it harms approved I-140 beneficiaries facing backlogs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Rick Bassett
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period unless DHS provides clear and comprehensive guidance concerning the legal consequences of employment termination.

The proposed rule would substantially change the treatment of workers whose employment ends before the expiration of their previously authorized period of stay.

However, the NPRM does not adequately explain how the proposed change would interact with the distinct legal concepts of nonimmigrant status, period of authorized stay, unlawful presence, removal proceedings, and eligibility for subsequent immigration benefits.

These concepts have different statutory and regulatory consequences and should not be treated as interchangeable.

DHS should clearly explain:

1. The precise date on which an affected individual would be considered to have failed to maintain nonimmigrant status following employment termination.
2. Whether the expiration of the existing grace period and the expiration of the previously issued Form I-94 have different legal consequences.
3. How a timely filed petition or application requesting an extension of stay or change of status would affect the individual's period of authorized stay.
4. How the proposed rule would interact with the unlawful-presence provisions of INA §212(a)(9)(B).
5. Whether and under what circumstances an affected individual could become subject to removal proceedings under INA §237(a)(1)(C)(i).
6. How USCIS would adjudicate subsequent petitions and applications when the prior employment terminated before the filing date.

The agency must not leave workers and employers to assume that every consequence of a failure to maintain nonimmigrant status occurs automatically on the same date.

The distinction is critical because individuals may face different legal consequences depending on their Form I-94 expiration date, the timing and type of subsequent filing, applicable statutory exceptions, and the circumstances of their employment termination.

DHS should publish clear examples addressing common scenarios, including an H-1B worker terminated while the I-94 remains valid, a worker whose new employer files a petition shortly after termination, and a worker who files a timely change-of-status application.

The absence of such clarification creates substantial uncertainty for workers, employers, and immigration practitioners and risks inconsistent adjudication.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposal unless it can provide a legally precise and administratively workable explanation of these consequences.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the grace period.

I support the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period. I am concerned about fraudulent educational credentials and employment histories in the H-1B program, and about employers using the program to replace higher-paid American workers with lower-paid labor.

In my view, employment-based immigration status should remain tied to the qualifying employment for which it was granted. I support removing this grace period, alongside stronger verification of credentials and work histories and enforcement of wage and worker-protection requirements.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to reconsider eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period.

Employment-based visa holders are often viewed through immigration benefits and employment sponsorship. However, their broader economic contribution is often overlooked. They are taxpayers, homeowners, consumers, investors and customers of American businesses. Their contributions support industries, local businesses, American jobs and government revenues.

>> THE ECONOMIC CONTRIBUTION EXTENDS TO THE ENTIRE HOUSEHOLD
Consider an H-1B professional who establishes a life in America. Beyond earning a salary and paying taxes, their household generates economic activity across numerous industries:
>>> Housing: Home purchases, mortgages, property taxes, insurance and maintenance.
>>> Education: School expenses, college tuition and university fees.
>>> Automotive: Vehicle purchases, financing, fuel, registration and insurance.
>>> Healthcare: Employer-sponsored health insurance premiums and medical expenses.
>>> Retail: Groceries, clothing, electronics, furniture and household necessities.
>>> Travel and hospitality: Airlines, hotels, restaurants and entertainment.
>>> Financial services: Bank accounts, mortgages, investments and retirement savings.
>>> Local businesses: Restaurants, childcare, transportation and home improvement services.
These expenditures generate business revenue, support American jobs, produce tax revenue and strengthen local economies. Every mortgage payment, tuition payment, vehicle purchase and grocery bill supports American businesses & workers.

>> ECONOMIC CONTINUITY PROTECTS AMERICAN BUSINESSES AND JOBS
When a visa holder unexpectedly loses employment, the impact extends beyond one employee. An entire household's spending, investments, insurance payments, educational expenses and participation in local businesses may disappear from the American economy.
A limited transition period allows experienced professionals to pursue other qualifying employment opportunities and continue contributing. Preserving this flexibility helps employers retain specialized talent, avoid recruitment disruptions and maintain household economic activity.

>> LABOR PROTECTIONS AND REGULATORY COMPLIANCE
Employment-based visa holders operate under structured labor and immigration regulations. For example, H-1B employers must generally comply with Department of Labor prevailing-wage or actual-wage requirements, whichever is higher. Many work in specialized, highly compensated roles, contributing through income taxes, payroll taxes and consumer spending. They also undergo background checks and navigate extensive immigration requirements, creating strong incentives to maintain lawful status and comply with applicable laws.

>> SOCIAL SECURITY AND MEDICARE CONTRIBUTIONS
Employment-based visa holders contribute to Social Security and Medicare through payroll deductions, alongside federal and state income taxes. These contributions help finance essential American public programs.

>> CONTRIBUTIONS TO AMERICA'S RETIREMENT AND FINANCIAL SYSTEMS
Many visa holders contribute to employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, often with employer matching contributions. These investments support American retirement providers, financial institutions, investment funds and capital markets.

>> IMMIGRATION SERVICES ALSO SUPPORT AMERICAN EMPLOYMENT
Immigration processing sustains government and contractor employment through USCIS offices, U.S. embassies and consulates, visa centers and regional biometric appointment centers. This ecosystem supports jobs in: Immigration processing & administration, Biometric enrollment & identity verification, Security screening & fraud prevention, Consular & visa application services, Customer support, IT and cybersecurity, Facilities management, logistics and operations, and Compliance & auditing.
These functions require human judgment, accountability and physical operations. A well-functioning immigration system can sustain employment and create opportunities for Americans in government and eligible contractor roles, even as AI and automation transform other industries.

>> CONCLUSION
Immigration policy should recognize the broader economic relationship created when employment-based visa holders and their families build their lives in America. Their contributions support American economy, local businesses, revenue services and support jobs. The 60-day grace period provides a limited opportunity to preserve these contributions when employment unexpectedly ends. Retaining it supports economic continuity, American businesses and the jobs connected to them. These professionals do not simply work in America; they invest, spend, pay taxes and contribute to the prosperity of American communities.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to reconsider this proposal. Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to reconsider eliminating the grace period, highlighting the economic contributions of visa holders.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364). Over ten years ago, my family and I came to the United States under legal nonimmigrant status. We have built our entire lives here, paid taxes, contributed to our local community, and raised our children in American schools. Eliminating the 60-day grace period would cause an immediate, catastrophic crisis for my family if my employment were to unexpectedly end.

Uprooting a family that has lived in a country for more than a decade cannot humanely be executed overnight. Our lease or mortgage commitments, car loans, and banking infrastructure cannot simply be dissolved in a matter of days. Furthermore, forcing children to abruptly leave their schools, their teachers, and their friends in the middle of an academic year will cause severe and lasting emotional and educational trauma.

Most critically, this rule fails to account for children with exceptional medical vulnerabilities. One of my children has special needs and relies on a highly coordinated network of local medical specialists, behavioral therapies, and individualized school accommodations. Continuity of care is vital for special needs children. Abruptly terminating our legal status without a grace period would immediately cut off access to these life-essential therapies. Finding, vetting, and transitioning to a new specialized medical team in another country takes months of planning. Forcing a special needs child into an immediate relocation is a safety hazard that threatens their developmental progress and physical well-being.

The current 60-day grace period is not a luxury; it is a critical humanitarian buffer. It allows legal nonimmigrants who face sudden job loss a baseline dignity to either find new employment or responsibly wind down their lives, break contracts, pull children from schools safely, and transition fragile medical care. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and maintain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing catastrophic impacts on their family.

This is turning employers to slaves, and it hurts both the immigrants and the US. Closing doors to global talents only sets the US back.

comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for employment-based visa holders.

Losing a job is already stressful enough. Forcing someone to leave the country immediately after a layoff, often through no fault of their own, is unnecessarily harsh and serves no practical purpose.

Sixty days is not an unreasonable amount of time to find another job. Job searches, interviews, background checks, and immigration paperwork all take time, especially in today's job market. Eliminating this grace period would make it much harder for qualified professionals to move between employers and would create unnecessary disruption for American businesses trying to hire them.

It also gives employers even more leverage over foreign workers, who may feel pressured to tolerate unfair working conditions because losing their job could immediately threaten their ability to stay in the country. Families and dependents would suffer the consequences as well.

The current grace period is already discretionary. USCIS has the ability to evaluate individual circumstances without taking this protection away from everyone.

This change would create far more harm than benefit. Please keep the existing 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to oppose the proposed removal of the up-to-60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

1. Job loss is usually not the worker's choice. Layoffs, restructurings, and project cancellations happen without warning. Under this proposal, a worker who has followed every rule would fall out of status the day their employer ends the job. That penalizes the employee for a decision they had no control over.

2. It undermines the portability Congress intended. AC21 and the 2016 high-skilled worker rule were designed to let skilled workers move between employers. Without a grace period, a new employer has no realistic window to prepare and file a petition. Portability would exist on paper but be unusable in practice.

3. It harms families and U.S. communities. Dependents, including children enrolled in U.S. schools, would have to leave immediately. Families would be forced to break leases, sell homes and cars at a loss, and pull children out mid-year. Landlords, lenders, schools, and local economies absorb those costs too.

4. It hurts U.S. employers. Employers would lose the ability to hire experienced talent already in the U.S. and integrated into the workforce. They would face higher costs and delays, and that talent may move to competing countries.

5. Case-by-case discretion is not an adequate substitute. DHS reports over 1.9 million filings involving grace-period assessments since FY2018. That shows how heavily workers and employers rely on this rule. Replacing a clear, uniform standard with individual discretionary requests would add uncertainty and adjudication burden for USCIS.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the current grace period. If DHS proceeds, it should at minimum provide a transition period and a meaningful window for workers affected by involuntary termination.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the removal of the grace period, citing harms to workers, families, and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Saurabh Deopura
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders and their dependents.

The proposed elimination of this protection would create unnecessary hardship for thousands of highly skilled professionals and their families who contribute significantly to the United States economy.

1. Protecting workers during unexpected employment disruptions

Employment termination can happen unexpectedly due to company restructuring, layoffs, economic downturns, mergers, or circumstances beyond an employee’s control. Losing a job should not immediately place an individual and their family at risk of losing their ability to remain in the United States.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a reasonable transition period to find another sponsoring employer, secure a new position, and pursue an eligible change or extension of immigration status.

2. Protecting families and dependents

This proposed change does not just affect the principal visa holder. It also affects spouses and children who have built their lives in the United States.

H-4 spouses and children, for example, may have established careers, education, healthcare arrangements, financial commitments, and community relationships. Eliminating the grace period could force entire families into uncertainty because of an employment decision they had no control over.

Children should not have their education disrupted, and spouses should not face sudden uncertainty about their ability to remain with their families.

3. Creating unnecessary pressure on skilled workers

Eliminating the grace period would place enormous pressure on foreign professionals to accept employment offers under unfavorable conditions simply to avoid losing their immigration status.

This creates an imbalance between employers and employees and could expose workers to exploitation, unfair compensation, and poor working conditions.

4. Negative impact on the U.S. economy

The United States benefits from retaining experienced professionals in technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and other critical industries.

These professionals have invested years in education, training, professional development, and contributing to American businesses. Eliminating the grace period could push talented professionals out of the country, resulting in lost productivity, increased recruitment costs, and the loss of valuable institutional knowledge.

5. Administrative efficiency should not come at the expense of families

If USCIS believes administering the existing grace period creates complexity, the appropriate solution is to improve processing, provide clearer guidance, and establish consistent eligibility criteria.

Eliminating this protection entirely is disproportionate to the administrative challenges identified by DHS.

My recommendations:

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to:

* Withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
* Preserve protections for spouses and dependent children.
* Maintain flexibility for individuals experiencing involuntary job loss or unexpected employment termination.
* Consider improving administrative procedures rather than removing an essential transition protection.

The 60-day grace period is not an automatic guarantee of continued employment or permanent immigration status. It is a reasonable opportunity for individuals and families to navigate unexpected employment disruptions while pursuing lawful immigration options.

Immigration policies should protect the integrity of the immigration system while also recognizing the human, economic, and family consequences of sudden employment loss.

I strongly urge USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardships for skilled workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
$103,265 for an H-1B? Protecting American jobs is absolutely a legitimate goal. But a six-figure price tag is the wrong tool for the problem.

The real question shouldn’t be, “How much can we charge for a foreign worker?” It should be: “Why is a company choosing to hire this person in the first place?”

The U.S. already has an important safeguard: H-1B employers must pay the higher of the prevailing wage or the actual wage paid to similarly qualified employees. H-1B workers are also protected by federal wage and labor laws.

Instead of imposing an enormous blanket fee, why not address the root causes?

1. Target genuine skill shortages.

Build a data-driven H-1B system focused on occupations and locations where the U.S. demonstrably lacks enough qualified talent. Require employers to show genuine efforts to recruit domestically before sponsoring international workers. Prioritize specialized roles where domestic supply cannot meet demand, rather than applying blanket restrictions across industries.

2. Strengthen wage protections and enforcement.

If companies are using H-1B workers to reduce labor costs, address that directly. Improve wage transparency, conduct regular audits and require employers to demonstrate that sponsored workers are paid competitively with similarly qualified American employees. Penalize companies that suppress wages or violate labor laws.

3. Address labor arbitrage, not legitimate talent mobility.

If companies exploit visa dependency, excessive working hours or outsourcing arrangements to obtain cheaper labor, regulate those practices. European employment protections, for example, establish equal-treatment requirements for temporary agency workers, including pay and working conditions. The U.S. should strengthen protections against exploitation rather than assume that foreign talent itself is the problem.

4. Make companies demonstrate the need for specialized talent.

For targeted occupations, require employers to explain why a position is difficult to fill domestically and what specialized skills or experience the candidate brings. Simultaneously, invest in American STEM education, apprenticeships, reskilling and workforce development to close long-term skill gaps.

5. Use reasonable, targeted fees—not a six-figure barrier.

A reasonable fee can fund enforcement, domestic training and workforce development. But a $103,265 charge risks creating the opposite outcome: companies may relocate jobs, hire abroad or move operations offshore. That doesn’t necessarily create more opportunities for Americans; it may simply move those opportunities elsewhere.

Companies don’t spend months recruiting, relocating and sponsoring international professionals for no reason. They do it because they believe those individuals bring specialized skills, experience, expertise or productivity that their business needs.

That doesn’t mean every H-1B hiring decision is justified. Employers should absolutely be held accountable for exploiting workers, suppressing wages, bypassing qualified American candidates or abusing the program.

But the solution should target the behavior, not punish every employer and every highly skilled professional with a six-figure barrier.

Let’s address the root cause of the hiring decision instead of simply making international hiring prohibitively expensive.

Protect American workers.
Close genuine skill gaps.
Punish labor abuse.
Ensure fair wages.
Invest in American talent.

Don’t mistake a $103,265 price tag for a workforce strategy.

America can protect its workforce AND remain a destination where the world’s best talent wants to build, innovate and contribute.

Those goals are not mutually exclusive.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (proposed removal of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2))

I'm asking DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

I live in Michigan, I work full time, and I'm a wife and a mother of two young children. I'm writing from the other side of this rule — the spouse's side — because when people talk about a worker losing status, they rarely talk about what happens to the rest of the family standing right next to him.

When a principal worker loses his job, his spouse often loses hers too, on the very same day. Many of us work lawfully on dependent status. We have our own employers, our own teams, our own responsibilities, and our jobs can be going perfectly well. Under this proposal none of that matters. His layoff ends my right to work as well. One company's decision would cost our family both incomes at once, and would leave my employer scrambling to cover my work with no notice and no handover — even though my employer did nothing wrong, and neither did I.

That is the part I can't get past. A household can plan for a lot of things. It cannot plan for both parents becoming unemployed and out of status on the same day, with no window at all to sort it out.

Health care sits in the middle of all of this. For most families like ours, health insurance comes through an employer. Losing a job is already frightening on that front. Losing status the next day is something else entirely. It leaves no time to finish a course of treatment, refill prescriptions, move medical and dental records, or find out what happens to a child who sees the same pediatrician for everything. Sixty days doesn't solve a health problem, but it lets a family hand things over properly instead of simply disappearing from the care they were in the middle of.

There is also the quiet, everyday life that never makes it into a Federal Register notice. Our children have teachers who know them, classrooms where they feel safe, friends they expect to see on Monday. Families like ours volunteer at school, show up, pay our taxes, and put down roots because we were told that playing by the rules mattered. The grace period was part of those rules for almost ten years. Taking it away overnight tells families that none of that counted for much.

I also think about the message this sends to the families who haven't come yet. Talented people choose where to build their lives. A spouse deciding whether to move her whole family across the world looks at stability as much as salary. If the answer is that one layoff means both parents lose everything in 24 hours, many families — especially mothers — will simply choose a country that treats them with a little more basic fairness. America loses those families long before any petition is filed.

None of us is asking to stay forever, or to work without permission. The grace period allows no work by the principal worker, and it lasts 60 days at most. All it really says is that a family gets a short, orderly window: to find a lawful next step, or to close out a life here with dignity — jobs handed over, care transferred, children prepared, goodbyes said.

A family should not have to vanish between a Tuesday and a Wednesday. Please keep the 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Workers

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to retain the existing provision under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). It gives eligible workers reasonable time to determine their next steps.

Employment can end for reasons beyond an employee’s control, including restructuring, project cancellations, budget reductions, or workforce changes. For H-1B workers, job loss also creates immigration uncertainty.

Finding suitable employment takes time. The process involves interviews, assessments, approvals, and immigration documentation. Without the grace period, workers could be required to leave the United States before completing promising interviews or receiving an offer. They may be forced to make rushed decisions without enough time to evaluate a position or lawful options. Retaining the grace period supports orderly transitions.

Impact on Families

The consequences of job loss extend beyond the individual. Many H-1B workers have spouses and children who have established their lives in the United States, with housing, school, childcare, healthcare, and other responsibilities.

Eliminating the grace period could require families to make immediate decisions about relocation, travel, and children’s education. Children may have to leave school during a term, and families may need to end leases or arrange an international move with little notice. These disruptions can create emotional and financial strain.

The grace period gives families time to understand their options and make informed plans.

Impact on Employers and the U.S. Workforce

H-1B professionals contribute specialized skills in technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and other fields. They may remain qualified to contribute to another organization even after losing a position.

The grace period gives prospective employers time to consider hiring these professionals and coordinate the necessary immigration process. Eliminating it may discourage employers from considering candidates when there is insufficient time to complete required steps. This could mean losing experienced professionals, disrupting projects, and increasing recruitment needs. Retaining the grace period supports workforce stability.

Financial and Emotional Hardship

Families often have ongoing expenses such as housing, transportation, insurance, childcare, education, and daily living costs. Sudden unemployment places these commitments under pressure. A quick departure may also involve travel and relocation costs, lease termination, and household arrangements.

The period provides time to assess options, manage finances, and plan responsibly. Removing it could intensify hardship and create uncertainty for individuals who did not choose to lose their jobs.

A Practical and Balanced Approach

I recognize the importance of an immigration system that is clear and compliant. The grace period is limited; it does not provide permanent status, guarantee new employment, or remove the obligation to follow immigration rules. It recognizes that employment transitions and related administrative steps are not always immediate.

If DHS has concerns about administration or compliance, these could be addressed through clearer guidance on eligibility, documentation, and requirements rather than eliminating the provision. This would preserve a reasonable safeguard while maintaining compliance responsibilities.

Request

I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period and retain the existing provision under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). It provides flexibility during unexpected employment changes, supports families, helps employers retain qualified professionals, and allows workers to pursue available options responsibly.

Eliminating the grace period could cause avoidable hardship for workers and dependents while creating challenges for employers and the broader workforce. A limited transition period is a reasonable balance between immigration compliance and the realities of employment.

Thank you for considering this comment. I respectfully urge DHS to preserve the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period and urges DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose eliminating the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). A worker who loses a job needs some time to find a new employer and get a petition filed. DHS has not shown that removing that time would save enough administrative work to justify the harm to workers, their families, and employers.

DHS points to more than 1.9 million filings since FY 2018 that USCIS potentially had to screen for the grace period. However, it says it cannot estimate how much time that review adds to each case.[1] Its Table 3 shows about 5,300 filings a year within the grace-period window in FY 2021-2025.[2] Neither number shows how much work repeal would save. Officers would generally still need to establish when the previous job ended, to decide whether the worker maintained status before the new filing. The payroll records DHS calls hard to interpret would be the same records.[1] DHS should estimate separately the time spent screening cases, establishing termination dates, and exercising discretion.

The accounting statement lists annualized costs as not estimated.[3] DHS's own example puts one worker's lost wages at up to about $21,900, which is two months of a $131,000 median wage. Applied to the 3,795 workers a year whose new employers filed within the window, that comes to about $83 million a year.[2] That figure covers only one group and assumes no more than two extra months without pay. DHS's broader proxy counts an average of 65,752 workers a year who left or changed jobs, and it misses some workers because not every classification requires an employer withdrawal.[2] DHS acknowledges losses to working spouses, broken leases, and other departure costs but does not quantify them. It treats departure costs as merely accelerated.[2] A family that must leave at once may also have to take a child out of school mid-year or sell a home on short notice.

For a worker laid off before the petition's validity period ends, the 10-day period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(1) does not help; DHS says it applies only after the validity period ends.[4] Without the grace period, that worker would generally be out of status the day after the job ends, even if another employer is ready to hire. An H-1B employer generally needs a certified Labor Condition Application before filing, and the Department of Labor has up to seven working days to decide on one.[5] H-1B portability lets an eligible worker start a new job once a qualifying petition is filed before the authorized stay expires.[6] DHS should explain how a laid-off worker could still use that provision under the proposal.

DHS acknowledges that workers and employers have made plans, including home purchases, around the current rule. It calls that reliance misplaced because the grace period is discretionary.[7] Workers cannot count on the full 60 days, but that alone does not show that the benefits of repeal outweigh its costs. DHS says many cases might receive the grace period, yet it gives no figures on how often the period is granted, shortened, or denied.[8] Those figures matter for both reliance and the claimed burden.

DHS considered a shorter period and stricter evidence requirements. It did not consider a fixed grace period without case-by-case discretion.[9] H-1B employers already must notify USCIS when employment ends.[10] A fixed period could start on the reported termination date, give workers a way to correct errors, and keep enforcement for fraud and other violations. Dates would still need checking. But this would remove the discretionary review DHS calls burdensome and preserve time to change jobs.

DHS should keep the grace period. Before proposing repeal again, it should measure the work it expects to save, estimate the costs, and evaluate a fixed period.

References:

[1] DHS, USCIS, [Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/11/2026-18631/eliminating-the-discretionary-60-day-grace-period), 91 Fed. Reg. 57807 (Sept. 11, 2026), §IV.C & nn.29–30 (pp. 57814–15).

[2] Id., §V.A.2–3, Tables 3–4 & nn.48–49, 54 (pp. 57820–23). $21,877 × 3,795 ≈ $83.0 million is my calculation from DHS's figures.

[3] Id., Table 2 (pp. 57817–18).

[4] Id. at 57812 n.16.

[5] 8 CFR 214.2(h)(4)(i)(B)(1); 20 CFR 655.740(a)(1).

[6] 8 U.S.C. § 1184(n).

[7] 91 Fed. Reg. at 57815–16 & nn.31–34.

[8] Id. at 57814.

[9] Id. at 57816 (§IV.E).

[10] 8 CFR 214.2(h)(11)(i)(A).
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the grace period, citing harm to workers, families, and employers.

Here is a stronger, concise version under 3,000 characters that retains the key arguments and emotional impact.

I strongly oppose the proposed 60-day grace period and urge the government to reconsider this policy because of its severe impact on law-abiding legal immigrants and their families.

Many of us have legally lived and worked in the United States for 10 years or more. During this time, we have followed all immigration rules, paid federal and state taxes, maintained legal employment, purchased homes, raised children, and contributed to our communities and the American economy. The United States is not just a temporary workplace for us; it is our home.

Unexpected job loss can happen to anyone due to layoffs, company restructuring, budget cuts, or economic conditions. Finding a new qualifying job within 60 days is extremely difficult, even for highly skilled professionals with years of experience. Recruitment processes involve multiple interviews, background checks, employer approvals, and immigration paperwork, all of which can take several months.

The impact goes far beyond the individual losing employment. Entire families are affected. Children attend schools, build friendships, and grow up considering the United States their home. Spouses may also have jobs, and families have established financial and personal commitments.

Relocating an entire family internationally within 60 days is simply unrealistic. Many of us own homes with outstanding mortgages. Selling a house alone can take several months. Families also need to sell vehicles, settle financial obligations, close accounts, arrange international shipping, manage personal belongings, and make arrangements for their children’s education. How can anyone reasonably be expected to find a new job, sell a house, settle years of financial commitments, and relocate an entire family in just two months?

After investing 10 years or more building a life in this country, being forced to abandon everything because of an unexpected employment situation is extremely harsh and unfair. It creates tremendous emotional, financial, and psychological stress for families, especially young children who have no control over these circumstances.

Legal immigrants contribute significantly to this country through income taxes, property taxes, Social Security, Medicare, homeownership, consumer spending, and professional skills. We have made long-term investments and commitments because we believed that following the law and contributing to society would allow us to build a stable future.

We are not asking for special treatment or exemption from immigration laws. We are asking for fairness, compassion, and a reasonable opportunity to find new employment without putting our families’ futures at risk.

I respectfully request the government to:

1. Extend the grace period from 60 days to at least 180 days.
2. Consider individuals’ years of lawful residence, employment history, and family circumstances.
3. Provide additional flexibility for families with dependent children and significant financial commitments.
4. Account for employer hiring timelines and immigration processing delays.

Please remember that behind every immigration case is a real person, a family, children, a home, and years of hard work and sacrifice.

A 60-day deadline cannot reasonably accommodate the realities of finding employment or relocating an established family internationally. Immigration policies should balance regulatory requirements with fairness and humanity.

Please reconsider this proposal and provide legal immigrants who have spent years contributing to America with a reasonable opportunity to protect their families and continue building their lives in the United States.

comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to remove the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other work-visa holders who lose their jobs. Reasons are as follows:

- Leaving the same day isn’t realistic or practical. Under the proposal, workers and their families would have to leave the day the job ends. Layoffs can come with little or no notice, so many people would fall out of status almost immediately through no fault of their own.
- The proposal treats someone who arrived last week on an H-1B the same as someone who has lived here for a decade or more. That person may own a home, have children in school, and be stuck waiting on a green card purely because of the severe backlog and for no fault of their own. The Supreme Court has said agencies must weigh this kind of reliance even when a policy is discretionary.
- There is no realistic chance to apply for another status. A laid-off worker would be out of status the next day. That leaves no window to apply for a change of status, or for the hardship work permit available to people with an approved I-140. This applies even to people who have an approved I-140 and have declared their intent to stay permanently and lawfully.
- Medical care is ignored. Some families are in the middle of medical treatments, a high-risk pregnancy, dialysis, recovery from surgery, or therapies for a child. They would have to stop with no time to arrange care elsewhere.
- The costs aren’t counted. DHS didn’t estimate the total cost and lists no costs at all to workers themselves, even though it acknowledges they buy homes, pay taxes, and put down roots. Legal fees, broken leases and mortgages, disrupted schooling, and future immigration problems are left out.
- The promised savings aren’t shown. DHS says the grace period creates extra work for officers, but admits it can’t measure how much. Officers will still need to check when a job ended, and DHS expects more deportation cases. The work shifts rather than disappears.
- Better options weren’t considered. DHS could keep the grace period for layoffs, protect people already here, including those with approved I-140s stuck in the backlog, or allow exceptions for medical and humanitarian cases.

Considering the huge potential cost and impact of this proposal to law-abiding families legally in the country, request DHS to reconsider this proposal. Alternatively, request publishing the real cost estimates first so that the public is provided an opportunity to review that data for public comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC)
comments.submitterName: Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC)
comments.commentText:
Public Comment in Strong Opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s Proposed Rule: Elimination of the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2))

This comment is submitted on behalf of the Associated Students of the University of California. As the student government representing all students at the University of California, Berkeley, we strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain employment-based non immigrant visa holders. We recognize that the proposed rule does not directly modify the grace period to F-1 international students but instead concerns the existing discretionary grace period available to certain employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders only. Nevertheless, we want to express our concerns regarding its potential impact on international employees at our campus and international students transitioning into the workforce.
International students make up approximately 15% of the student population at UC Berkeley. Beyond the student population, international faculty, researchers, postdocs and other specialized staff in classification covered in the rule have also long been an integral part of our campus community, and these individuals collectively made University of California one of the nation’s leading public universities system not only through academic excellence, but also bringing in innovative minds and educational opportunities. Therefore, we believe that opportunities should not end at the classroom door, nor should professional opportunities be limited by immigration uncertainty. However, we are concerned that the proposed rule would close the door to opportunities in a country that has long been recognized for its diversity and commitment to welcoming talent from around the world. We kindly ask the administration to carefully consider the unintended consequences of this proposed rule for the U.S. economy. Beyond these concerns regarding equitable academic and professional opportunities, we would also like to address specific aspects of the proposed rule:
We are concerned about whether eliminating the grace period would meaningfully reduce the administrative burden. One of DHS’s justifications for the proposal is to reduce the administrative burden by evaluating the eligibility of existing discretionary grace period (Sec. IV.C and IV.E). Contradictorily, it also acknowledges the possibility of additional Notices to Appear. We are concerned that eliminating the grace period may not necessarily reduce the overall administrative burden, but instead just shift the burden from USCIS to other federal agencies and the immigration courts, which are ultimately borne by taxpayers. We therefore ask DHS to provide a more comprehensive accounting of these potential costs.
We ask DHS to consider reasonable reliance interests of affected individuals and their families. DHS acknowledges that affected nonimmigrant workers and their dependents may have made significant career and personal plans in the existing 60-day grace period (Sec. IV.D; footnotes 32 and 34). Although the current grace period is discretionary, the removal may disrupt commitments made in reasonable reliance on the availability of current protection, especially for individuals with childcare responsibilities or other significant family obligations.
In Sec. IV.B, Sec. IV.E, footnote 26, it discussed about “otherwise authorized to lawfully remain” for individuals with pending immigration applications and those already within an existing 60-day grace period. However, there are no specific definitions of who counts as “otherwise authorized”. We therefore urge DHS to provide clear guidance on these circumstances, and to further evaluate less disruptive alternatives, such as a standardized or automatic grace-period framework, which would remove the case-by-case review it complains about.
Sincerely,
Associated Students of the University of California
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period.

I respectfully oppose this proposed rule. I am an H-1B worker in the technology sector, in the United States for over a decade, with an approved I-140 and an employment-based priority date that is still years from being current. My spouse is in H-4 status and we have two young children.

The 60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) is the only realistic bridge between jobs. A new employer cannot file an H-1B petition immediately: it must first obtain a certified Labor Condition Application from the Department of Labor, which alone takes about seven business days, and only then prepare and file the petition — several weeks in total. The figure of 1.9 million petitions does not isolate cases where the grace period was actually invoked, while the Department's proxy data shows approximately 18,975 new-employer Form I-129 petitions filed within the 60-day window — workers using the grace period for exactly its intended purpose: an orderly transition to a new sponsor. The assessment the Department describes is, by its own wording, an "additional initial assessment" — a preliminary determination, not a re-adjudication of the filing itself.

If DHS proceeds anyway, I ask at minimum that any final rule (1) apply only prospectively, to cessations after its effective date, (2) retain the grace period for workers with an approved I-140, and (3) preserve the grace-period reference relied on for compelling-circumstances employment authorization under 8 CFR 204.5(p).

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposal.

My perspective reflects both a deep commitment to regulatory compliance and first-hand experience with the realities of long-term integration.
1. Severe Disruption to U.S. Citizen Children and Families
For long-tenured residents—especially those facing decades-long green card backlogs with approved I-140 petitions—an abrupt job loss without a grace period directly destabilizes U.S. citizen children. Forcing a family into emergency departure or immediate loss of legal status creates profound humanitarian hardship:
Sudden disruption to U.S. citizen children enrolled in American schools and embedded in their local communities.
Forced, distress sales of long-term real estate, 401(k) accounts, and domestic financial assets under extreme time pressure.
Sudden termination of family healthcare coverage and residential leases or mortgages.
2. Economic Realities of Professional Recruitment and Filing Timelines
Job loss in high-skilled sectors stems from economic downturns, corporate restructurings, or project cancellations, not compliance violations. Finding a qualifying H-1B position requires several weeks to complete recruitment, multi-round technical interviews, background checks, Department of Labor (DOL) Labor Condition Application (LCA) certifications, and USCIS petition filings. Expecting a worker to execute an immediate transfer or departure overnight ignores standard administrative and industry timelines.
3. Protection of U.S. Business Interests and Economic Growth
The 60-day grace period is a practical bridge, not an unauthorized benefit. Retaining experienced talent within the U.S. supports American companies facing skill shortages. Forcing tax-paying, highly specialized professionals to abruptly leave—only for them to be re-hired and relocated back to the U.S. weeks later—imposes unnecessary administrative costs on U.S. businesses.
4. Discretionary Authority Provides Existing Regulatory Safeguards
The regulation under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) already grants USCIS full discretion to shorten or deny the grace period in cases involving status violations or bad-faith actions. DHS can maintain regulatory integrity using this existing mechanism without imposing blanket hardship on fully compliant families.

comments.commentText:
This supplements my earlier comment (tracking number mw0-3y50-sena). Some comments supporting the rule cite Table 3 as evidence that the grace period is being misused, however, this table doesn't support that conclusion.

DHS proposes removing the grace period to align the regulations with its reading of the statute and reduce administrative burden.[1] It doesn't present Table 3 as evidence of abuse. If DHS adopts that argument in the final rule, it should explain what evidence supports it and give the public an opportunity to respond.

DHS describes the grace period as a way to help workers change jobs and provide flexibility after job loss.[2] Table 3 records new-employer petitions for 2,138 workers in FY 2021 and 5,178 in FY 2025, with the count rising each year. Dividing by each year's beneficiary total gives 5.2%, 4.1%, 4.9%, 7.1%, and 7.5% for FY 2021–2025. The corresponding shares for Form I-539 applications were 0.6%, 0.2%, 0.8%, 2.7%, and 3.9%.[3] These are my calculations, rounded to one decimal place. Workers finding new employers within the window is the use DHS says the grace period was created for.

For the H-1B workers in the FY 2025 new-employer sample, the median wage offered was $131,000. DHS uses that figure to illustrate how a worker required to leave could lose up to about $21,900 in wages while searching for work and returning to the United States.[4] That analysis recognizes a practical use for the grace period: allowing a worker to move to another employer without first leaving the country. DHS thus treats these workers as people the rule would harm, not as evidence that the grace period is abused.

The table also leaves much unexplained. USCIS cannot distinguish resignations from terminations in these records.[5] More job losses could lead to more filings without any increase in misuse. Some workers are missing because their employers never filed withdrawals; others are included even though they changed jobs without using the grace period. The fiscal year is the year the old petition was revoked, which may differ from the year employment ended.[3][6] The percentages therefore do not measure actual grace-period use. The table gives no approval or denial rates, findings of fraud, or breakdown of I-539 applications by the status requested.

Nor does staying beyond 60 days necessarily mean a worker has violated the rules. DHS acknowledges that certain applications filed during the grace period may permit a worker to remain longer.[2]

Before relying on misuse as a reason for repeal, DHS should publish supporting evidence and take comment on it. Useful information would include decisions on filings made during the window, reasons for denial, and how often USCIS shortened or eliminated the grace period. Any count of workers remaining beyond 60 days should distinguish those with a lawful basis to remain from those without one. The increase in filings alone doesn't establish misuse.

References:

[1] DHS, USCIS, Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period, 91 Fed. Reg. 57807, 57808 (Sept. 11, 2026), https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/11/2026-18631/eliminating-the-discretionary-60-day-grace-period; see also id. at 57816.

[2] Id. at 57820.

[3] Id. at 57821 (Table 3 and source note).

[4] Id. at 57822 & nn.52, 54. The wage is the amount stated on the new petition and is not always verified after hiring (n.52).

[5] Id. at 57822.

[6] Id. at 57820 n.49.

Subject: Opposition to the Elimination of the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for non-immigrant workers. While I understand the agency’s administrative objectives, the total removal of this transition window inflicts severe, unnecessary hardship on long-term non-immigrant residents and their families who have built their lives, careers, and communities in the United States.

Non-immigrants on employment-based and other legal visas often live in the U.S. for years, contributing significantly to the economy, innovation, and local communities. Over years of residency, individuals and families naturally accumulate deeply integrated personal and financial responsibilities. An abrupt or absent grace period fails to account for the immense logistical complexity of winding down a life established over multiple years.

Specifically, eliminating this buffer creates major crises in the following areas:

Real Estate and Housing Commitments: Many long-term residents own homes, hold long-term residential leases, or have mortgages. Selling a home, breaking a lease without catastrophic financial penalties, or liquidating property cannot realistically be accomplished overnight.

Major Assets and Liabilities: Non-immigrants own vehicles, manage localized bank accounts, utilities, auto loans, and insurance policies. Unwinding these legal and financial obligations requires adequate time to avoid severe credit damage and financial loss.

Disruption to Children and Families: Families with children face profound upheaval. Kids enrolled in U.S. schools, sports, and local social circles require a thoughtful transition period. Forcing families out instantly without time to manage school transfers or emotional closures is deeply damaging to children.

Employment Transitions: The tech and corporate sectors experience frequent market shifts. When layoffs or status changes occur unexpectedly, highly skilled professionals need a reasonable runway to either secure alternative sponsorship or responsibly organize their departure.

The existing 60-day grace period is already a minimal window to handle these monumental life changes. Eliminating it entirely does not improve immigration integrity; instead, it penalizes law-abiding contributors who have invested years into their communities.

I urge USCIS to reconsider this proposal and preserve a realistic transition window that respects the human and logistical realities of long-term non-immigrant residency.

For years, this vital buffer has allowed professionals who experience unexpected layoffs or job transitions a reasonable window to secure new employment, file change-of-status petitions, or orchestrate an orderly departure. Stripping away this time frame means that any sudden change in employment status would instantly render skilled workers and their families out of status, effectively creating an atmosphere of chronic uncertainty. This proposal threatens to disrupt corporate mobility and talent retention across vital sectors like technology, healthcare, and engineering. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Prateek Khatri
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364; RIN 1615-AD22 — Comment Opposing "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (91 FR 57807, September 11, 2026)

I write as an H-1B nonimmigrant employed in a specialty occupation, and as a husband and father, to respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I have lived and worked in the United States lawfully, paying federal, state, and local taxes throughout. My wife holds H-4 status, and our two-year-old son was born here. We own our home, our son attends local daycare, and every part of our family's life was built in reliance on the stability the current regulatory framework provides — including the 60-day grace period.

The proposal treats the end of employment as an event affecting only the worker. In reality, it affects entire families. If my employment were to end unexpectedly — through a layoff or restructuring outside my control — the proposed rule would strip my wife and toddler of status the very next day, alongside me. We would face the choice of uprooting a two-year-old from his home, his daycare, and his pediatrician with zero transition time, or separating our family. Holding a temporary visa does not mean holding a temporary family. Skilled professionals on H-1B visas have spouses, children, mortgages, and deep community roots. The grace period recognizes that human reality; its elimination ignores it.

This proposal is particularly severe because, for many of us, there is no timely path to permanent residence. Employment-based green card backlogs stretch for years — in some cases decades — through no fault of the applicant. We cannot simply adjust our way out of a sudden job loss. The 60-day period is often the only bridge between an unexpected termination and a new petition, a change of status, or an orderly departure. Removing it does not accelerate any process; it only ensures that a layoff becomes an immediate status violation for people who have done everything the law asked of them.

Sixty days is already a narrow window. A prospective employer must prepare a Labor Condition Application, file a new H-1B petition, and navigate USCIS processing — a sequence that routinely consumes most or all of those 60 days even when every party acts in good faith. Eliminating the window does not make hiring faster; it makes lawful transition impossible, forcing skilled workers — along with their tax contributions, consumer spending, and institutional knowledge — out of the country over a timing technicality.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, the Department should preserve a transition period for workers and, critically, for their dependent family members — including U.S. citizen children — who bear no responsibility for an employer's staffing decision yet would suffer its most immediate consequences.

Respectfully submitted,
Prateek Khatri

I am a U.S. citizen with over ten years of professional experience, including five years as an aerospace engineer and five years in analytics consulting, and I hold an MBA. I write in support of the proposed rule to remove the discretionary 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

A grace period that lets a worker remain in status after that job ends separates the status from the very basis on which it was granted. The grace period serves a small share of workers at a large administrative cost (Sections IV.C and V.A). Effects on U.S. workers. In my industry, consulting and IT services firms rely heavily on employer-sponsored visa workers. When such a worker is laid off, the grace period lets them compete for new U.S. positions while remaining in the country, adding to a labor pool that already puts downward pressure on wages and advancement for U.S. citizens in these fields. Requiring departure upon job loss, with the option to seek readmission once a new employer files a qualifying petition, gives U.S. workers a fairer opportunity to fill those openings.
Reliance interests (Section IV.D). I agree with DHS that reliance on a discretionary benefit that USCIS could already shorten or eliminate is limited. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Supplemental comment on DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2))

I already sent in a comment on this docket earlier today, anonymously, against this proposal. This one is a supplement to it. A couple of things were still on my mind tonight that I did not get into the first comment, and there is one idea I wanted to add.

If DHS is set on changing the rule, here is a suggestion worth considering. Instead of getting rid of the grace period altogether, stretch it to 90 days, but make the extra time conditional and for leaving only. The way I see it, the normal window would work the way it does now, where a person tries to find a new employer or sort out a different status. If that does not happen, they could have up to 90 days in total if they can show they are actually getting ready to go. A house put on the market. A lease being closed out. A flight booked. Bills being paid off. Still no working during any of it, not one day. The extra time would have just one job, letting a family pack up a whole life here in a proper way. Anyone who has sold a house knows it can take a month or two from listing to closing, if it goes smoothly. Sixty days was never a lot of time for that. It was barely enough. And a conditional departure window would not cost the government anything. What it would do is cut down on the defaults, broken leases and empty houses that an overnight departure dumps on banks, landlords and neighbors here.

The other thing I keep coming back to is knowledge. Plenty of people in these visa categories have been here a long time. Ten years, fifteen, sometimes twenty. They learned their trade here. They were trained by American companies, hospitals and universities, and a lot of what they know is not written down anywhere. It is the stuff you only pick up by doing the work for years. Why a system was built the way it was. What breaks, and who you call when it does. If someone like that loses a job and has to be gone the next day, that knowledge does not pass to whoever replaces them. It just leaves with them, to Canada or the UK or India, and it builds up over there instead of here. We spent all those years developing that expertise in this country. Losing it because a new petition could not be filed fast enough seems like a waste that no one has really counted.

Then there is the money side, which the proposal does not talk about much. DHS itself puts the median pay for workers who use this grace period at around $131,000. Someone earning that is paying a lot of tax. Federal income tax and payroll taxes every year, state tax on top of that, property tax, sales tax, and money into Social Security and Medicare too. Now think about the roughly 3,795 workers a year in DHS's own estimate, and then think about the working years those people still have ahead of them. The taxes that leave with them add up to a very large amount of money. These are people in their best earning years whose employers here mostly want to hire them back within a few weeks. Pushing them out for good does not save the country money. It sends future tax revenue to some other country instead.

I said in my first comment that I think this proposal should be withdrawn, and I have not changed my mind. But between keeping 60 days and going to zero, zero is the wrong answer. If DHS wants a compromise, a conditional 90 days to leave in an orderly way is a reasonable one. I hope the agency will at least think about what walks out the door, in skills and in taxes, when skilled people get no real chance to stay.

Thank you for reading this.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the grace period and suggests extending it instead.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly oppose the proposed removal of the grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and retain the existing protection for eligible workers and their dependents.

Losing a job can happen unexpectedly because of layoffs, restructuring, or a business closure—circumstances outside an employee’s control. Workers should have a reasonable opportunity to respond responsibly, seek qualifying employment, explore available immigration options, or arrange an orderly departure.

Eliminating this transition period would create unnecessary hardship for families. Housing commitments, children’s schooling, medical care, and international relocation cannot reasonably be resolved immediately after an unexpected job loss. A temporary employment disruption should not force an entire household into an avoidable crisis.

I am also concerned about the consequences for American employers. Recruiting involves interviews, hiring decisions, and preparation of required paperwork. Removing the grace period could prevent employers from retaining qualified people who are already here and available to fill legitimate vacancies. DHS should carefully evaluate those practical costs.

The proposal could also increase workers’ dependence on their current employers. If losing a job means losing any meaningful opportunity to transition, workers may feel less able to report mistreatment or challenge unsafe or unfair working conditions. Preserving a reasonable transition period supports a healthier labor market.

DHS identifies reduced administrative burden as a justification for this change. I urge the agency to demonstrate why any savings outweigh the potential costs to workers, families, employers, and other government functions. Administrative convenience should not outweigh substantial, foreseeable disruption without a convincing evidentiary basis.

I support compliance with immigration law and clear eligibility requirements. A limited transition period helps people manage an unexpected job loss responsibly while pursuing lawful next steps.

Please retain the existing grace period and address any demonstrated concerns through targeted measures rather than eliminating this protection for everyone affected.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes removing the grace period and asks DHS to withdraw the proposal.
